title: Platform Design, Earnings Transparency and Minimum Wage Policies: Evidence from A Natural Experiment on Lyft

detail.title: Platform Design, Earnings Transparency and Minimum Wage Policies: Evidence from A Natural Experiment on Lyft

detail.abstract: We study the effects of a significant design and policy change at a major ridesharing platform that altered both provider earnings and platform transparency, examining how it altered outcomes for drivers, riders and the parent platform, and providing managerial insights about how to balance competing stakeholder interests while avoiding unintended consequences. In February 2024, Lyft introduced a policy guaranteeing drivers a minimum fraction of rider payments while also increasing per-ride earnings transparency. The rollout of this policy was staggered, first introduced in “major markets” that were more urban, providing a natural experiment to assess how platform transparency and earnings guarantees affect ridesharing availability, driver engagement and rider satisfaction. Using trip-level data from over 47 million rides in a major urban market and its neighboring suburban markets across six months, we applied dynamic staggered difference-in-differences models along with a geographic border strategy to measure the causal effects of these platform design changes on supply- and demand-side outcomes, ride production and platform outcomes. We show that the design change led to substantial changes in driver engagement, with separate effects from the guarantee and the transparency. Drivers increased their working hours and utilization, leading to more completed trips and higher per-hour and per-trip earnings. These effects were strongest for drivers with lower pre-policy earnings and greater income uncertainty. We unpack the economic mechanism by which these changes led to a positive spillover on demand. We also provide some evidence that points to platform transparency potentially leading to unintended strategic driver behavior. In ongoing work, we outline a counterfactual simulation framework that models ride production as a function of driver supply hours and rider intents, examining how small changes in driver choices might have amplified the positive effects of the intervention even further, and develop a self-supervised machine learning model that leverages driver trajectory embeddings to predict multihoming behavior and examine whether supply increases came from both the expansion of driver activity as well as substitution from competing platforms. Our study shows how platform-led interventions present an intriguing alternative to government-led minimum pay regulation, and provide new strategic insights into managing platform change.

detail.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption scales globally, the hidden environmental costs-manifested as significant energy consumption and "Ghost Carbon"-have become a critical national-scale challenge. title: Mirror Amplification Theory

detail.title: Mirror Amplification Theory
detail.abstract:
Mirror amplification is a cognitive mechanism that emerges from the continuous interaction between externalization (action) and AI‑based reflection (reaction). This reciprocal cycle forms a structural analogue to Newtonian mechanics: externalization functions as a cognitive force that accelerates understanding, while uninterrupted reflection preserves the momentum of thought. As a result, the user experiences a sustained and rapidly intensifying flow of insight.
The theory identifies mirror amplification as a new class of cognitive dynamics made possible by advanced AI reasoning systems. It explains how structured reflection, recursive questioning, and controlled ambiguity generate exponential cognitive acceleration. The phenomenon requires specific metacognitive skills, including granular externalization, structural reading of AI responses, and the ability to recursively transform reflections into new questions.
Mirror amplification provides a formal framework for understanding how AI‑mediated cognition can produce breakthroughs that are difficult to achieve through conventional reasoning. It offers a foundation for modeling AI‑human co‑thinking as a mechanical system of thought, revealing a new domain of cognitive physics.

title: Design and Evaluation of Reversible Data Hiding Techniques for Operational Technology Protocols
affiliations: Warsaw University of Technology and Warsaw University of Technology

detail.title: Design and Evaluation of Reversible Data Hiding Techniques for Operational Technology Protocols
detail.abstract: Operational Technology (OT) networks still rely on communication protocols that were never designed with security by default. This makes them vulnerable to various hiding techniques such as Reversible Data Hiding (RDH), which can conceal information without affecting the visible behavior of industrial traffic. This work presents how RDH can be applied to Modbus, IEC 60870-5104, and S7Comm by examining their inner workings in a simulated OT environment. The study demonstrates that implementing these protocols directly affects the ease with which hidden data can be inserted and later restored. The findings underscore that RDH may pose a genuine security concern for OT environments, highlighting the need for enhanced methods to detect and mitigate such activity. In particular, results show that explicit RDH methods offer higher reversibility at the cost of increased latency, while implicit methods provide better throughput but lower reliability

title: Dynamic Optimization for In-App Advertising Games: A Data-Driven Methodology Validated with Field Experiments
affiliations: HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong, HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong, The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics and Tencent Inc.

detail.title: Dynamic Optimization for In-App Advertising Games: A Data-Driven Methodology Validated with Field Experiments
detail.abstract: The mobile gaming industry is increasingly reliant on in-app advertising (IAA) revenue, with rewarded ads as a common model: players voluntarily watch an ad in exchange for an in-game item (e.g., lowering difficulty). This creates a key intertemporal trade-off—raising difficulty can drive more ad views and short-term revenue, but may also frustrate players, increase churn, and reduce lifetime value (LTV). The challenge is compounded by strong player heterogeneity and very high early churn, making slow-learning methods ineffective. This paper presents a deployed decision-making system that maximizes lifetime rewarded-ad revenue via dynamic difficulty adjustment (DDA). We formulate DDA as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with latent player types capturing heterogeneous skill and ad tolerance. To enable data-efficient learning and interpretability, we instantiate the POMDP with a structural econometric model of player behavior that links difficulty to win probability, ad-watching, and churn. We develop a practical estimation pipeline and an offline Monte Carlo planning approach that yields a compact policy suitable for real-time deployment. In two large-scale online A/B tests on production games, the agent increases lifetime ad impressions by 23.6% and 7.0%, while improving mid-to-late lifecycle retention (survival at level 300) by up to 204% and 297%.

detail.abstract:
Modern power is shifting from institutions and coercion to computational environments that shape behavior at speed and scale. Unlike state surveillance, which is visible and contestable, algorithmic environmental modification operates invisibly redesigning the incentive architecture of human decision-making itself. Our crisis is not just “misinformation”, but an incentive and tempo mismatch between silicon systems and biological governance.

I argue this mismatch has two components: a contingent political‑economic selection for extraction (surveillance advertising, VC growth curves, state surveillance permissiveness) and a structural velocity gap between algorithmic feedback loops and human institutions. Using systems ecology and cybernetics as analogical lenses, I model the resulting trophic inversion, temporal shear, and autoimmune polarization. The solution is metabolic architecture: constraints on incentives, propagation speed, data persistence, and independent observability implemented by many actors with exit (portability and interoperability) as the strongest lever.

detail.abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) with advanced code generation capabilities marks a distinct inflection point in software engineering. This paper argues that the traditional role of the "coder"-defined by the manual translation of logic into syntax-is rapidly becoming obsolete. In its place, a new paradigm is emerging: System Architecture as the primary unit of engineering value. Drawing on case studies from the development of *Gaari*, a distributed mobility platform, and *The Trail*, an intelligence system, this paper demonstrates that as syntax becomes commoditized, the engineering bottleneck shifts to system design, data flow coherence, and architectural resilience. We propose that the modern engineer must transition from a syntax-first approach to a logic-first "System Architect" model to remain relevant in an AI-driven ecosystem.

title: CARE: A Practical Governance Model for AI Deployment Decisions

detail.title: CARE: A Practical Governance Model for AI Deployment Decisions
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in operational, security, and decision-making contexts, organizations face a persistent governance gap: while existing frameworks identify and manage AI risk, they often leave deployment authority, ethical override, and accountability mechanisms undefined. This paper introduces CARE (Confirm, Align, Risk, Ethics), a lightweight governance model that structures AI deployment decisions through four independent review functions. CARE complements existing risk management frameworks, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, by governing whether an AI system should proceed to deployment rather than prescribing technical controls. CARE explicitly separates evidence verification, intent alignment, risk evaluation, and ethical assessment, prohibits score averaging, and grants ethical review override authority. The model is designed for zero-budget implementation using existing organizational roles and produces auditable decision records suitable for public-and private-sector oversight.

detail.abstract: Incorporating firm-and investor-level risks into discounted cash flow valuations of privately firms can noticeably reduce the estimated fair market value. Based on a literature review, five central risk factors are described that contribute to the private company discount. The results suggest that these factors can be conceptually grouped into principally systematic and unsystematic risks, that enhance the coherence of valuations. For both types, a refined multifactor cost of equity model is derived providing an alternative to the limited modified CAPM and build-up approaches. Based on stochastic simulations synthesizing existing studies, the two complementary models show an overall probabilistic range of 12% to 26% with a mean close to 16% to 19% for the required return of an average private firm, in which certain risks may be mitigated. This central tendency seems broadly in line with previous research.

title: The Right to Access Foreign Communicative Infrastructure

detail.title: The Right to Access Foreign Communicative Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Legal discourse needs to build on the right to access foreign ideas, extending it to the right to access foreign communicative infrastructure (like TikTok). My argument extends to all significant foreign communicative apps, including chatbot-centric apps. Political, economic, and cultural influences shape communicative apps, and each app amplifies different kinds of content and offers different ways to engage. Changing foreign apps’ ownership removes these influences and burdens speech in ways that judges should account for. The value of Americans’ right to access communicative infrastructure, including foreign communicative infrastructure, is under-considered in legal debate about communicative apps. The social media and Artificial Intelligence industries are structured such that newcomers struggle to break through and are almost always purchased by the dominant firms, as WhatsApp and Instagram were. These leaves online communicative infrastructure very vulnerable to capture by private power. Unsurprisingly, competitor apps are only able to emerge from protected markets in other states. Leaving reciprocal trade barriers aside and focusing on citizens’ access to multiple sources of information and modes of engagement, this means that without better market regulation in the United States, foreign communicative apps are an important source of alternative information, engagement, and competition.

title: Architecting Carbon-Aware Cloud Infrastructure: A Technical Implementation Guide using GCP How "Automated Resource Hygiene" and FinOps can drive the next wave of Sustainable AI

detail.title: Architecting Carbon-Aware Cloud Infrastructure: A Technical Implementation Guide using GCP How "Automated Resource Hygiene" and FinOps can drive the next wave of Sustainable AI
detail.abstract:
As the global demand for Artificial Intelligence (AI) accelerates, the environmental footprint of the underlying cloud infrastructure has reached a critical inflection point. This paper proposes a novel framework for Carbon-Aware Cloud Architecture specifically engineered for the Google Cloud Platform (GCP) ecosystem. Moving beyond static offsets, this research introduces the concept of “Automated Resource Hygiene”—the integration of real-time carbon intensity telemetry with automated Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) triggers to optimize workload scheduling and regional placement.

The framework bridges the gap between FinOps (Financial Operations) and GreenOps, demonstrating that cost-optimization and carbon-reduction are synergistic rather than competing priorities. Through a technical deep dive into GCP-native tools—including the Carbon Footprint API, BigQuery, and GKE Autopilot—we demonstrate how organizations can implement "temporal shifting" and "spatial migration" to align high-compute AI training jobs with periods of peak renewable energy availability.

Experimental results indicate that by automating resource lifecycle management and applying carbon-intelligent scaling policies, enterprises can achieve a significant reduction in operational carbon intensity (gCO2eq/kWh) without compromising service level objectives (SLOs). This guide provides cloud architects and DevOps engineers with a scalable blueprint for building the next generation of energy-efficient AI systems, establishing a new standard for sustainable digital transformation in the hyperscale era.

title: Radical Responsibility as an Inner Infrastructure of Sustainable Leadership

detail.title: Radical Responsibility as an Inner Infrastructure of Sustainable Leadership
detail.abstract: Sustainable and responsible leadership frameworks increasingly emphasize long-term value creation, ethical decision-making, and stakeholder orientation. In organizational practice, however, these frameworks often remain fragile precisely in those situations where they matter most: under pressure, in conflict, and in conditions of uncertainty. What becomes visible across many leadership contexts is that implementation gaps are less a consequence of missing structures or models, and more a reflection of how leaders internally respond to stress, ambiguity, and perceived loss of control. Building on literature from Sustainable and Responsible Leadership, Self-Leadership, and organizational psychology, this paper suggests Radical Responsibility as an inner infrastructure of sustainable leadership. Radical Responsibility is understood as the capacity to consciously assume ownership of one’s perceptions, emotional reactions, and behavioral choices, even when external conditions cannot be controlled. Methodologically, the paper follows a theory-informed conceptual synthesis combined with reflective practitioner insight. Rather than offering empirical proof, it seeks to clarify underlying mechanisms and translate them into real-world leadership practice. The paper outlines pragmatic leadership practices that illustrate how Radical Responsibility can stabilize responsible leadership behavior in everyday organizational life and provides a conceptual foundation for future empirical research.

title: Automated Strategy Discovery in Crypto Perpetuals via Dynamic Factor Ensembles and Auditable Evaluation

detail.title: Automated Strategy Discovery in Crypto Perpetuals via Dynamic Factor Ensembles and Auditable Evaluation

detail.abstract: Offline backtests are a central evaluation tool for data-driven decision policies, yet their apparent performance can collapse when evaluation mismatches deployment semantics (delays, costs, cash-flow accounting) or when repeated search reuses the same windows. We study automated strategy discovery in cryptocurrency perpetual futures, where fees, slippage, and funding cash flows can dominate profit and loss (PnL) for high-turnover policies. We present an end-to-end protocol that (i) maintains a dynamic, compact factor pool to control feature combinatorics, (ii) searches a modular policy family under STRICT T+1 execution with explicit cost and funding accounting, and (iii) selects configurations via robustness screening (cost stress) and walk-forward evaluation while exporting deterministic, machine-readable artifacts and invariant checks for auditability. From a knowledge-based systems perspective, the protocol represents evaluation semantics and selection rules as explicit knowledge objects, enabling traceable decision support and review. Across four liquid perpetual contracts (BTC/USDT, ETH/USDT, SOL/USDT, AVAX/USDT), we show that fee-only or zero-cost assumptions materially inflate apparent performance relative to a fully costed configuration. Under identical STRICT semantics, two-stage robustness screening tends to reduce drawdowns. Our contribution is validation infrastructure rather than a claim of persistent alpha: the protocol makes offline-to-deployment gaps and selection bias easier to detect, reproduce, and review.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that all social relations are fundamentally oriented toward individual interests, though such interests are often unconscious, symbolically mediated, or culturally obscured. I contend that the concept of "authentic relations" functions as a normative construction designed to legitimate patterns of cooperation, reduce uncertainty, and stabilize interactions within complex social systems. The thesis is grounded in evidence from evolutionary biology, incentive economics, the sociology of power, philosophy of action, and historical analysis of social formations. Through multidisciplinary analysis, I demonstrate that instrumentality constitutes a structural constant in human relations, while authenticity represents a recent and culturally contingent rhetorical device. My theoretical framework integrates adaptationist mechanisms, transaction cost reduction, symbolic performance, and historical analysis to reconceptualize the foundations of human cooperation.

title:
Firm Dynamics and Intergenerational Mobility
Does Adolescent Exposure to Young Firms Shape Long-Run Outcomes?

detail.title:
Firm Dynamics and Intergenerational Mobility
Does Adolescent Exposure to Young Firms Shape Long-Run Outcomes?
detail.abstract: Why do two children from nearly identical family backgrounds end up in such different economic circumstances as adults? This paper investigates a largely unexplored dimension: whether the timing and location of labor market entry drive long-run differences in intergenerational mobility. As Part II of a companion study (Part I: “Entrepreneurial Exposure with Intergenerational Mobility” by Kian Foshee), this analysis extends from tract-level entrepreneurial exposure to county-by-cohort entry environments, asking: do young adults entering markets during periods of dynamic hiring and favorable industry composition achieve systematically higher economic mobility? Using Opportunity Insights county-by-cohort mobility data merged with Quarterly Workforce Indicators, I exploit within-county, across-cohort variation in entry conditions (ages 18–20) to relate adult income-rank outcomes for children from 25th-percentile families to net job growth, hiring dynamics, and sectoral hiring shares. Preliminary estimates suggest that changes in hiring predict mobility more strongly than levels and that industry composition matters substantially: a 10 percentage-point increase in the service-sector share of hiring is associated with roughly 0.5 rank points higher mobility, while a 10 percentage-point increase in high-growth sector share is associated with about 0.3 rank points higher mobility (under baseline county clustering). Event-study patterns indicate that conditions at ages 19–20 are at least as predictive as age 18, consistent with heterogeneous entry timing and early match formation. Robustness checks highlight key identification limits: significance is sensitive to more conservative clustering, unweighted specifications can flip signs, and effects concentrate in large, already high-mobility counties. Accordingly, Part II is best read as reduced-form evidence on the early-career opportunity window and candidate channels that can discipline (and motivate) future causal designs linking firm type to mobility.

detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping how organizations make decisions, allocate resources, manage risk, and exercise authority. Once confined to analytical support roles, AI systems are now embedded within core governance processes, influencing prioritization, compliance, performance evaluation, and strategic direction across both private and public institutions. While existing research has extensively examined the technical performance, fairness, and explainability of AI systems, far less attention has been given to the governance consequences of delegating decision influence to algorithmic systems.
This paper examines ethical AI from a governance-centered perspective, arguing that the primary challenge posed by AI is not technological, but institutional. Drawing on real-world scenarios from leading AI-developing and AI-adopting organizations, the study explores how automation alters traditional decision structures, diffuses accountability, and challenges long-standing assumptions about transparency and responsibility. It highlights a growing disconnect between the speed and scale of AI-assisted decision-making and the capacity of existing governance mechanisms to provide effective oversight.
The paper proposes a human-centered framework for ethical AI governance that balances three interdependent dimensions: automation, accountability, and transparency. Rather than treating ethics as a property of algorithms alone, the framework positions ethical governance as a continuous organizational practice, requiring explicit decision rights, traceability of AI-influenced outcomes, and meaningful human oversight. By reframing AI ethics as a leadership and governance imperative, this research contributes to a broader understanding of how organizations can harness AI’s capabilities while preserving trust, legitimacy, and human responsibility.
The findings are relevant to executives, policymakers, governance professionals, and scholars seeking to navigate the ethical and organizational implications of AI-enabled decision-making in complex institutional environments.

title: Weyl-Taste Utility: Unifying Geometry, Attention, and Dynamic Choice

detail.title: Weyl-Taste Utility: Unifying Geometry, Attention, and Dynamic Choice
detail.abstract: Classical utility theory assumes that preferences can be represented by a scalar potential function, implying that the utility dierence between two consumption bundles is independent of the path taken between them. This assumptionmathematically equivalent to the marginal-utility vector eld being a gradientis violated by substantial experimental evidence showing that experienced utility depends on consumption sequences, not just endpoints. We develop a unied theoretical framework that generalizes classical utility by allowing marginal utilities to form a one-form that need not be exact. The failure of exactness is measured by curvature, a gauge-invariant geometric quantity. When curvature is nonzero, utility becomes genuinely path-dependent: the same endpoint can yield dierent utility levels depending on how it was reached. This paper makes ve contributions: (1) We provide complete mathematical foundations with explicit regularity conditions and prove that curvature is the unique observable quantity characterizing path dependence. (2) We derive a precise bridge to classical demand theory via a reference-path scalar utility, showing that curvature manifests as Slutsky matrix asymmetry and structured GARP violations. (3) We establish a cognitive microfoundation: cross-inhibitory attention dynamics generically induce nonzero curvature, connecting our framework to the psychology of constructed preferences. (4) We prove a separation theorem that enables empirical identication of curvature distinct from taste drift, and provide a complete experimental protocol. (5) We solve a two-good general equilibrium model completely, showing that curvature creates oscillatory but stable price dynamics. The paper provides rigorous mathematical foundations with explicit regularity conditions. Proofs are complete where indicated; where we provide sketches, this is noted explicitly. Examples are worked through to closed form where feasible. We also provide an honest discussion of limitations and open challenges.

detail.title:
Re-Engineering Inland Transport Risk: 
A System-Powered Inspection Stack for Tail-Risk Detection in Indian Over-Dimensional Cargo Movement
detail.abstract:
Inland transport risk across Indian road networks is predominantly assessed through post-loss claims data, insurer loss runs, and retrospective survey reports. While these approaches provide historical visibility, they fail to capture structural risk formation during cargo movement—particularly for Over-Dimensional Cargo (ODC) and Over-Weight Cargo (OWC), where losses emerge from system interactions across routes, carriers, loading practices, and operational governance rather than isolated events.

This white paper introduces a System-Powered Transport Risk Inspection Stack, grounded in inspection-first data rather than claims-first data. Using anonymised inspection outputs from 2025 ODC/OWC movements across Indian inland roads, the study demonstrates how structured inspection protocols, operational SOPs, and network-level analytics enable earlier detection of tail risk, exposure concentration, and delay amplification—well before losses crystallise.

A multi-layered analytical framework separates shipment frequency, monetary exposure, and tail delay behaviour (P90 delays) across carriers, routes, and consignees. Concentration risk is quantified using shipment- and exposure-based Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI) measures, while interaction effects are visualised through carrier–route heatmaps and exposure–delay risk maps. All entity identifiers—including consignors, consignees, carriers, and GSTINs—are deterministically anonymised to preserve analytical integrity without compromising commercial confidentiality.

Findings show that ODC/OWC risk is rarely proportional to shipment volume alone. Instead, loss potential clusters around specific combinations of operational behaviour, route constraints, and governance gaps—patterns largely invisible in conventional claims datasets. By integrating live industrial SOPs, the paper demonstrates how inspection-driven controls materially reduce tail risk when embedded upstream, repositioning inspections as foundational infrastructure for preventive transport risk governance rather than reactive loss documentation.

detail.abstract: Girls and women living in urban slums face far greater challenges than their counterparts in more stable environments. Limited access to quality education, poor parental support, neglect, and restrictive cultural norms expose them to heightened risks of exploitation, including involvement in sex-work and early unintended pregnancies; conditions that perpetuate cycles of vulnerability and poverty. As a result, pregnant girls and women in this marginalized environment encounter multiple health, social, and economic difficulties that severely compromise maternal and child health outcomes. This paper examines the pivotal role of health literacy and healthy living as transformative tools for empowering vulnerable pregnant girls and women in urban slums. It contends that enhancing knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors around reproductive health, personal hygiene, nutrition, and healthcare access can serve as a sustainable strategy for breaking cycles of poor health and social inequality. The study also emphasizes the importance of culturally-sensitive, community-based interventions that equip marginalized women and girls with the information, skills, and resources needed to make informed decisions about their health and well-being. detail.abstract: Drip pricing-gradually revealing fees during checkout-is prevalent in online ticketing and has drawn regulatory scrutiny. The FTC's Junk Fees Rule (December 2024, effective May 2025) now requires upfront total price disclosure for event tickets and short-term lodging. However, empirical evidence on consumer response to alternative pricing formats in ticketing remains limited. We conducted a between-subjects experiment with 467 US consumers comparing three formats: all-in pricing (fees included), drip pricing (fees at checkout), and transparent pricing (fees shown upfront). Results reveal that pricing format significantly affects perceived fairness (F(2,464) = 19.10, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.70). Drip pricing rated below the 7-point scale midpoint (M = 3.87 vs. neutral = 4.0), indicating consumers perceive it as unfair. All-in pricing (M = 5.03) outperformed both drip and transparent (M = 4.32) approaches. Critically, 67-75% of participants expected fees, yet drip pricing was still judged unfair-fee expectation does not neutralize negative perception. These findings provide timely empirical support for the FTC's intervention. Results suggest mandatory all-in disclosure may be more effective than transparency requirements alone, as consumers rate all-in significantly higher than transparent pricing (Δ = 0.71, p < .001). Practical implications for industry compliance and consumer welfare are discussed.

title: The United States' Employment-Based Immigration System: An Analysis of H-1B Worker Backlogs, Policy Shortcomings, and Reform Pathways

detail.title: The United States' Employment-Based Immigration System: An Analysis of H-1B Worker Backlogs, Policy Shortcomings, and Reform Pathways
detail.abstract: The U.S. employment-based immigration system traps over 1.8 million skilled workers and their families in legal limbo due to outdated quotas and per-country limitations that have remained unchanged for thirty-five years. The Immigration Act of 1990 established a ceiling of 140,000 employment-based green cards annually combined with a rigid seven-percent per-country cap that allocates the same number of visas to India (population of 1.4 billion) as to Iceland (population of 400,000). These provisions have generated wait times as extreme as 195 years for Indian nationals in the EB-2 category, with over 400,000 projected to die before obtaining permanent residency. This backlog, along with its induced dependence on temporary work visas, creates three cascading harms. First, employer-specific sponsorship combined with high switching costs-$5,000+ in fees and multi-year delays-concentrates labor-market power among employers and suppresses H-1B wages by 12.2% through constrained mobility. Second, it traps H-4 dependent spouses, over 90% of whom hold bachelor's degrees, in years-long employment prohibition, artificially removing skilled labor from the workforce. Third, it forces many children to age out at 21, creating deportation risks for those who are American in every meaningful sense except paperwork. Four complementary reforms can collectively address this crisis. First, phasing out the seven-percent per-country cap would gradually transition visa allocation from nationality-based limits to a demand-driven system, allowing applicants from high-demand countries to advance in the backlog without causing abrupt increases in wait times for those from low-demand countries. Second, increasing the annual employment-based visa ceiling would alleviate the overall shortage that persists regardless of allocation methods. Third, dependent exemption would exclude spouses and minor children from counting toward the annual cap, ensuring that all 140,000 visas are allocated to independently qualified principal workers rather than divided among family members. Fourth, visa recapture would reclaim approximately 339,000 unused visas from prior years, delivering immediate backlog relief under existing statutory authority while longer-term structural reforms advance through Congress. These reforms would close the widening gap between America's need for skilled talent and its statutory capacity to receive it.

Importantly, digital literacy acts as a significant mediating mechanism linking emotional intelligence to productivity, emphasizing the need for organizations to strategically cultivate both competencies in synergy. The study advances the theoretical discourse on employee productivity by conceptualizing the integrated roles of emotional and digital competencies and provides actionable insights for organizations to design holistic human resource development initiatives that align with the rapidly digitalized and dynamic characteristics of contemporary work environments.

continuity rather than scale-driven expansion. It argues that sustainable performance in
unstable markets depends on the integration of adaptive marketing capability, risk-aware

a strategic sensing and coordination function that links firm-level adaptation with broader
market stability.

can remain viable and relevant under sustained volatility. Rather than treating instability as a
condition to be corrected, the paper demonstrates how responsible adaptation at the
organizational level contributes to resilience at the market level.

a non-crisis-based interpretation of growth under uncertainty. It is intended for scholars,
strategists, and decision-makers seeking to understand how growth, risk, and stability intersect

title: Music Streaming and Royalty Protection in Nigeria: The Limits of the Copyright Act 2022

detail.title: Music Streaming and Royalty Protection in Nigeria: The Limits of the Copyright Act 2022
detail.abstract:
Music streaming has fundamentally transformed how Nigerians consume recorded music, yet the legal framework governing this transformation remains inadequate. This study examines the limits of the Copyright Act 2022 in protecting streaming royalties for Nigerian musicians, revealing a significant gap between statutory language and practical enforcement. While Section 10 of the Act grants authors the right to communicate their works to the public by wire or wireless means, language broad enough to encompass digital streaming, the Act does not define streaming platforms, specify their licensing obligations, establish royalty calculation methods, or mandate transparent data reporting. This silence has left Nigerian artists without reliable mechanisms to verify usage, challenge underpayment, or enforce their rights.
The study adopts a doctrinal methodology, examining the Copyright Act 2022 alongside international treaties including the Berne Convention, the WIPO Copyright Treaty, and the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty, and undertaking comparative analysis of approaches in the United States, the United Kingdom, and South Africa. The research finds that the United States addressed similar challenges through the Music Modernization Act 2018, which established the Mechanical Licensing Collective to administer blanket mechanical licences and maintain a public database of musical works and rights holders. The United Kingdom relies on well-established Collective Management Organisations such as the Performing Right Society for Music (PRS for Music) and Phonographic Performance Limited (PPL), though concerns about fairness persist. South Africa demonstrates that African CMOs can succeed through direct licensing arrangements and multi-territorial hubs, as evidenced by the Composers, Authors and Publishers Association (CAPASSO).
By contrast, Nigerian CMOs operate without clear statutory guidance, transparent governance structures, or effective regulatory oversight, resulting in delayed payments, opaque royalty statements, and widespread artist dissatisfaction. The study concludes that Nigeria must introduce express statutory provisions defining streaming platforms and their obligations, clarify how royalties should be divided between songwriters, performers, and producers, strengthen CMO governance through mandatory transparency and accountability measures, establish effective enforcement mechanisms including statutory damages and specialised tribunals, and facilitate cross-border royalty collection through regional cooperation frameworks such as the African Continental Free Trade Area Protocol on Intellectual Property Rights.
These reforms are essential not only to bring Nigeria into compliance with its international obligations under the WIPO treaties and the TRIPS Agreement, but also to ensure that the promise of copyright protection translates into tangible financial security for the creators whose labour sustains the Nigerian music industry. Without such reforms, the Copyright Act 2022 will remain what scholars have described as an empty promise, offering recognition in law but failing to deliver the economic reward that copyright was designed to guarantee.

title: Gender Dimensions of SME Tax Compliance: Evidence, Institutional Dynamics, and Policy Implications

detail.title: Gender Dimensions of SME Tax Compliance: Evidence, Institutional Dynamics, and Policy Implications
detail.abstract:
Tax compliance among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) remains a persistent policy challenge in developing and emerging economies, where limited administrative capacity, informality, and uneven access to information constrain revenue mobilization and equitable growth. Within this context, growing scholarly attention has been directed toward understanding how gender-related factors influence compliance behavior; however, findings remain fragmented across jurisdictions and institutional settings. This study undertakes a structured review and synthesis of the literature on gender-focused and institutional tax compliance, drawing on empirical and conceptual studies conducted across multiple countries and regulatory environments. Using a systematic approach to source selection and thematic analysis, the review integrates evidence from prior research on SME tax behavior, enforcement mechanisms, and taxpayer education programs. 
The synthesis reveals consistent gender-related differences in tax knowledge, compliance attitudes, risk perception, exposure to sanctions, and responsiveness to both educational initiatives and enforcement strategies. In several contexts, female SME owners and managers demonstrate higher compliance propensities linked to risk aversion and normative considerations, while male counterparts often exhibit greater tolerance for enforcement risk. However, these patterns are neither universal nor deterministic. The findings indicate that gender does not operate as a standalone determinant of SME tax compliance; rather, its influence is mediated by institutional quality, access to education, digital literacy, enforcement credibility, and prevailing social norms .
The study concludes that effective SME tax policy must move beyond gender-neutral assumptions. From a policy perspective, the evidence supports the adoption of gender-responsive tax education programs, context-sensitive enforcement designs, and transparent administrative mechanisms that account for institutional and social heterogeneity. Such approaches can enhance voluntary compliance while promoting fairness and inclusivity in SME taxation systems.

title: Trend Following in Strategic Asset Allocation:  A Long-Horizon Analysis and Retail-Oriented Implementation

detail.title: Trend Following in Strategic Asset Allocation:  A Long-Horizon Analysis and Retail-Oriented Implementation
detail.abstract:
Traditional portfolio construction frameworks rely on static asset allocation and cross-asset diversification to manage risk and improve long-term outcomes. Well-known approaches such as the All-Weather Portfolio and the Permanent Portfolio aim to reduce drawdowns and volatility through fixed exposures to multiple asset classes.

These frameworks have demonstrated robustness across a wide range of economic environments and remain a cornerstone of long-term portfolio construction. At the same time, recent literature has highlighted that portfolio risk is not solely determined by asset class composition, but also by the time-varying nature of market regimes and return dynamics.

This paper investigates the role of trend following as a structural component of strategic asset allocation, rather than as a standalone return-seeking strategy. Using long-horizon historical data, we examine whether systematic trend-based exposure management can complement traditional diversification by addressing risk from a different dimension: the temporal evolution of market trends.

The results suggest that incorporating trend following as a structural overlay can provide a complementary form of diversification—one based on time and regime dynamics rather than asset classes alone—potentially improving portfolio efficiency and resilience without relying on return forecasting or discretionary market timing.

This study contributes to the asset allocation literature by framing trend following not as a substitute for traditional diversification, but as a systematic tool for enriching multi-asset portfolio construction in changing market environments.

title: Jurisdictional Sovereignty: A Consent-Based Critique of Divine Authority

detail.title: Jurisdictional Sovereignty: A Consent-Based Critique of Divine Authority
detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel philosophical framework for evaluating theological claims of authority by applying consent-based political philosophy to the domain of divine command. Rather than engaging the traditional ontological question of God's existence, I propose a jurisdictional approach that treats the legitimacy of divine authority as analytically separable from questions of divine ontology. Drawing on social contract theory, I argue that the capacity to create rational agents does not inherently generate the moral authority to govern those agents. I term this position jurisdictional sovereignty-the principled refusal to grant legislative power to any entity, regardless of its ontological status or creative role, without demonstrable consent-based legitimacy. This framework is distinguished from atheism (which addresses existence), apatheism (which expresses indifference), and misotheism (which expresses antagonism), offering instead a political evaluation of authority claims. I defend this position against sophisticated theological objections, particularly those emerging from classical theism, and demonstrate its applicability across diverse religious frameworks. The framework has direct implications for political philosophy, grounding bodily sovereignty and public reason requirements without presupposing metaphysical naturalism.

detail.abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) represent a novel organizational paradigm operating across multiple regulatory jurisdictions without traditional legal personhood, exposing participants to significant liability and enforcement risk. This study constructs a comprehensive quantitative taxonomy of regulatory frameworks applicable to DAOs, analyzing 72 operational entities across seven jurisdictional models and examining enforcement actions from fiscal years 2024-2025. We formalize the regulatory compliance burden as a multi-dimensional optimization problem, model liability distribution as a function of governance participation and token holdings, and derive metrics for securities classification risk and anti-money laundering exposure. Data aggregated from Wyoming DAOLLC/DUNA implementations, UK Limited Liability Partnership proposals, Malta ITAS certifications, Swiss Foundation structures, and the emergent Harmony Framework reveal that DAOs without legal wrappers exhibit 3.2× higher expected liability costs and face 4.7× greater regulatory enforcement probability. The proposed four-tier classification system-Unregistered Protocol DAOs, Operational Wrappers, Foundation Structures, and Hybrid Multi-Jurisdictional Entities-accounts for 94% of observed variance in regulatory outcomes. Regression analysis indicates that legal personhood recognition reduces member-level risk exposure by 68% while imposing median compliance costs of $127,000 annually. Securities enforcement data from 2024-2025 demonstrate that DAOs distributing governance tokens without exemption frameworks face prosecution rates of 23%, compared to 2.8% for legally structured entities. This framework provides a tractable model for jurisdictional selection, compliance architecture design, and governance mechanism optimization under regulatory uncertainty.

title: Demographic Ageing and Economic Growth in India: Threshold Evidence from a Discrete Regression Model

detail.title: Demographic Ageing and Economic Growth in India: Threshold Evidence from a Discrete Regression Model
detail.abstract: India's demographic landscape is shifting as the share of the elderly in the total population rises, potentially undermining its long-standing demographic dividend. While demographic ageing has been widely studied, the possibility of nonlinear growth effects remains underexplored in the Indian context. This study addresses that gap by applying a Discrete Threshold Regression model to annual data from 1960 to 2023, testing whether a critical threshold exists in the old-age dependency ratio (OLDDEPR) beyond which its relationship with GDP per capita growth changes fundamentally. Results reveal a statistically significant threshold at a log OLDDEPR of 1.94 (approximately 7%) around 1977, marking a structural break in India's growth dynamics. Below this threshold, ageing has minimal impact on growth. Beyond it, ageing significantly constrains GDP per capita, despite the continuing demographic dividend. Interaction effects show that higher domestic savings can buffer this drag, while rising consumption exacerbates it. This is the first empirical application of threshold regression to the ageing-growth nexus in India, offering evidence of a demographic tipping point and highlighting the nonlinear macroeconomic effects of ageing. These findings provide actionable insights for policymakers: boosting long-term savings and rebalancing consumption will be essential to sustaining growth in an ageing economy.

title: Multimodal Urban Itineraries under Budget and Time-Window Constraints: A Real-World Application in Istanbul

detail.title: Multimodal Urban Itineraries under Budget and Time-Window Constraints: A Real-World Application in Istanbul
detail.abstract: The steady growth of urban tourism has created a demand for sophisticated decision-support tools capable of navigating complex metropolitan environments. However, existing itinerary planning models often neglect the operational realities of modern travel, such as the synchronization of mandatory meal breaks, multimodal transportation feasibility, and trade-offs between budget and time. In this study, we introduce the Multimodal Tourist Trip Design Problem (MTTDP), a rich variant of the orienteering problem constructed using real-world operational data from an industrial partner in Istanbul. To address the combinatorial complexity of the MTTDP, we develop a tailored Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) framework. Our approach is rigorously evaluated not only against exact methods and a Memetic Algorithm (MA) benchmark but also through a component-level ablation study using Shapley values to quantify the operator contribution. Computational experiments in realistic instances demonstrate that the proposed ALNS scales effectively when exact methods fail, improving the coverage of the itinerary by up to 60% in large-scale scenarios compared to the results obtained by a commercial solver under a time limit.

title:
The Manifesto of Omittoism

A Jurisdictional Declaration of Human Sovereignty

detail.title:
The Manifesto of Omittoism

A Jurisdictional Declaration of Human Sovereignty
detail.abstract:
"The Manifesto of Omittoism" speaks to those who feel stranded between the rigid dogmas of religion and the cold silence of atheism-a group it identifies as "The Philosophical Orphans." It proposes that for centuries, humanity has been trapped in a vertical debate over whether God exists, missing the far more vital political question: by what right would such a being rule? 

The text argues that we have confused power with authority. Just as we eventually learned that a King's army does not give him the moral right to own his subjects, Omittoism asserts that a Creator's power does not give Him the moral jurisdiction to command our private thoughts or demand our worship. By conducting a forensic audit of the universe-examining the immense suffering, structural flaws, and infinite threats found within it-the manifesto concludes that the entity in charge, if He exists, has failed the basic standards of legitimate governance. 

Consequently, this work serves as a formal declaration of independence. It outlines a way to build a meaningful, ethical life not by looking up for orders, but by looking across at one another with empathy and reason. It describes the transition of the human species from fearful subjects waiting for a savior into responsible citizens who have finally accepted the beautiful, terrifying liberty of governing themselves.

title: Concentrated Liquidity as Exotic Options: Optimal Range Selection and Dynamic Hedging in Automated Market Makers

detail.title: Concentrated Liquidity as Exotic Options: Optimal Range Selection and Dynamic Hedging in Automated Market Makers
detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive options-theoretic framework for analyzing concentrated liquidity positions in automated market makers (AMMs), with particular focus on Uniswap v3. We establish that a concentrated liquidity provider (LP) position within a specified price range is mathematically equivalent to a portfolio comprising the underlying asset and a short position in a perpetual power straddle with barrier features. We derive closed-form expressions for the Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega) of LP positions and characterize the distribution of impermanent loss under geometric Brownian motion. Our main contribution is the derivation of an optimal range selection rule under mean-variance preferences, providing explicit formulas for the optimal lower and upper bounds as functions of volatility, fee tier, risk aversion, and investment horizon. We further develop a dynamic hedging strategy that allows LPs to neutralize directional exposure while retaining fee income. Comparative statics reveal that optimal ranges contract with increasing volatility and expand with higher fee tiers, consistent with economic intuition. Extensions to jump-diffusion and stochastic volatility environments are provided. Our theoretical framework offers practical guidance for liquidity providers seeking to optimize capital efficiency in decentralized exchanges.

title: Beyond Terrestrial Limits: Japan's Orbital Solar Transmission Test and the Emergence of Post-Planetary Energy Systems

detail.title: Beyond Terrestrial Limits: Japan's Orbital Solar Transmission Test and the Emergence of Post-Planetary Energy Systems
detail.abstract: Japan's 2025 demonstration of wireless power transmission from space marks a pivotal moment in the evolution of global energy systems. For the first time, a satellite in low Earth orbit successfully collected solar energy, converted it into microwave radiation, and transmitted it to a terrestrial receiver where it was reconverted into usable electricity. This essay examines the demonstration as a civilizational inflection point, confirming the technical feasibility of space-based solar power (SBSP) and opening pathways toward scalable orbital energy infrastructure. The analysis explores the physics of microwave transmission, the economic logic of scaling orbital arrays, the safety and governance frameworks required for global deployment, and the broader implications for planetary resilience and long-horizon civilizational engineering. Japan's achievement is interpreted as the first operational step toward post-terrestrial energy abundance and the billion-year frontier of human development.

title: As US Food Aid Retreats, can BRICS+ and Biotechnology Fill the World’s Food Security Gap?
affiliations: Korbel School of International Studies, University of Denver

detail.title: As US Food Aid Retreats, can BRICS+ and Biotechnology Fill the World’s Food Security Gap?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Policy Brief 26-4
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Cuts to agricultural development assistance and food aid by the United States and other advanced economies are creating a global vacuum just as climate change and conflict drive global hunger up. Many food-insecure developing economies with significant hunger lack the resources to self-finance agricultural research and development (R&D) and have had to depend increasingly on themselves—and one another—to meet rising food needs. Hendrix argues that the BRICS+ economies—Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, and Indonesia—are well positioned to fill the world’s food security gap.

Key Takeaways
For BRICS+, the stakes are existential because hunger and climate vulnerability are clear domestic challenges, not distant risks. Investments in climate-resilient, regionally adapted crop research would provide self-insurance and also help stabilize neighboring fragile states, where food insecurity drives migration.

The returns to investments will be greatest if they are accompanied by science-based regulatory reforms. Governments of economies wary of biotechnology should educate the public and reform regulations to reap the benefits of advanced agricultural technologies.

BRICS+ have the scientific know-how, institutional capacity, and capital to underwrite a massive increase in public agricultural R&D funding. Doing so would be an opportunity to demonstrate that they are capable of providing global leadership.

title: Machine Learning-Enhanced GIS for Predictive Disaster Risk Analytics

detail.title: Machine Learning-Enhanced GIS for Predictive Disaster Risk Analytics
detail.abstract: This study explores the integration of machine learning (ML) with geographic information systems (GIS) to enhance predictive disaster risk analytics. The research employs GIS-based spatial analysis in combination with advanced ML models, including AutoML and deep learning algorithms, to assess and predict risks associated with floods, landslides, and wildfires. By leveraging historical hazard data, environmental parameters, and socioeconomic indicators, the integrated framework enables high-resolution risk mapping and scenario simulation. Key findings indicate that ML-enhanced GIS models significantly improve prediction accuracy compared to conventional methods, optimize resource allocation, and reduce emergency response times in multi-hazard scenarios (Gao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, the approach demonstrates scalability across different geographic regions and hazard types, providing decision-makers with actionable insights for proactive disaster management. The study concludes that the fusion of ML and GIS constitutes a robust and adaptable framework capable of supporting anticipatory planning, risk mitigation, and evidence-based policy development in disaster-prone areas (Thangamayan et al., 2024). These findings underscore the potential of data-driven, intelligent spatial analytics to transform conventional disaster management strategies into proactive, precision-oriented interventions.

title: Meaning, Passion Health™, and Performance: A Multidimensional Framework for Sustainable Human Performance

detail.title: Meaning, Passion Health™, and Performance: A Multidimensional Framework for Sustainable Human Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it is a conceptual and integrative analysis that did not involve new data collection from human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Decades of research across psychology, organizational behavior, and neuroscience indicate that sustained human performance cannot be explained by pressure, incentives, or effort alone. While such factors may generate short-term output, they are consistently associated with long-term declines in engagement, wellbeing, and performance sustainability. Increasingly, research suggests that meaning plays a central role in regulating how individuals engage with work, persist through challenge, and sustain performance over time. This paper presents an integrative framework that conceptualizes meaning as a multidimensional, functional system arising from the interaction of internal inclination, perceived significance, and personal preference. Drawing on established research in self-determination theory, work engagement, harmonious passion, psychological safety, and job design, the paper synthesizes fragmented literatures into a coherent model of meaning as a regulatory mechanism for human performance. The framework is further grounded by findings from the Passion Health™ Study, an applied mixed-methods research initiative involving 2,170 respondents across professional and educational contexts. Directional associations observed between multidimensional conditions of passion, engagement, and performance provide empirical support for the proposed model. By reframing meaning as a diagnosable and operational construct rather than an abstract ideal, this paper offers a practical architecture for understanding performance degradation, burnout, and disengagement. Implications for organizational design, leadership, and future research are discussed.

The full stimulus item set, training materials and instructions are provided to assist other researchers who are interested in using the task and methodology in other work.

title: The Generative Theory of the Sensation-Behavior Cycle: A New Paradigm of Life Empiricism

detail.title: The Generative Theory of the Sensation-Behavior Cycle: A New Paradigm of Life Empiricism
detail.abstract: Contemporary mind science has reached an impasse over the "hard prob-lem" of consciousness, facing the predicament of data-rich yet theoreti-cally fragmented. This paper proposes the "Generative Theory of the Sensation-Behavior Cycle," achieving a fundamental paradigm shift: from abstract speculation about "consciousness" to the study of life itself as a generative process of the "Youjue System." The theory takes the Sensation-Behavior Cycle as its basic unit and Value-Dependent Selec-tion as its core mechanism, constructing the Three-Dimensional Dy-namic Taxonomy of Youjue Sensation to systematically explicate the emergent path of mind from the Vital Stratum, Social Stratum to Noet-ic Stratum, and revealing the unified generative logic running through all strata ── "Resonance-Evaluation-Consolidation." Based on this, the paper thoroughly reconstructs core concepts such as memory, cogni-tion, need, emotion, consciousness, self, and will from a generativist per-spective, and creatively reinterprets classic research. More importantly, the paper explicitly elaborates on the methodological revolution of "Life Empiricism" ── grounding itself in irreducible first-person facts, tak-ing subject-internalization and change as the criterion of validation, and regarding traditional scientific data as corroborative traces of the subject's state. This theory aims to provide a powerful meta-theoretical framework for life science, achieving seamless interpretation from neural activity to civilizational structure, and opening new integrated paths for mind re-search.

title: Evaluating the Role of GIS Dashboards in Real-Time Crisis Management

detail.title: Evaluating the Role of GIS Dashboards in Real-Time Crisis Management
detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization, the increasing frequency of natural disasters, and the growing complexity of emergency response have created a critical need for effective crisis management tools (Damaševičius et al., 2023). This study evaluates the effectiveness of Geographic Information System (GIS) dashboards in supporting real-time decision-making during emergencies (Han & Choi, 2024). Employing a mixed-methods approach, the research integrates case studies, system evaluations, and quantitative analyses of response times and decision accuracy. Findings indicate that GIS dashboards significantly enhance situational awareness, streamline communication, and reduce response times, thereby improving coordination among multiple stakeholders (Bond, 2024; Villani et al., 2023). However, the study also highlights that the benefits of such dashboards are contingent on factors including the accuracy and timeliness of data, user training, and seamless integration with existing emergency management systems. These insights underscore the potential of GIS dashboards to strengthen real-time crisis response while emphasizing the need for careful implementation and ongoing evaluation.

title: Geospatial Analysis of Resource Allocation Efficiency in Emergency Services

detail.title: Geospatial Analysis of Resource Allocation Efficiency in Emergency Services
detail.abstract:
Emergency service systems increasingly face challenges related to inefficient resource allocation, delayed response times, and unequal service coverage, particularly across diverse urban and rural contexts. These challenges are exacerbated by population growth, spatial expansion of cities, and rising demand for emergency care. In response, geospatial analytics and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have emerged as critical tools for enhancing evidence-based decision-making in emergency management (Park, Kwon, and Azam; Mansourihanis et al.). Despite growing adoption, empirical assessments of how advanced GIS techniques improve response efficiency and equity remain limited.
This study applies GIS-based spatial analysis, accessibility modeling, and comparative evaluation techniques to assess emergency response coverage and resource distribution across heterogeneous geographic settings. Using network analysis, service area modeling, and spatial equity metrics, the study evaluates baseline emergency service performance and compares it with scenarios incorporating advanced GIS workflows and Next Generation 911 (NG911) data integration (Alamri; He et al.).
The findings reveal pronounced spatial inequalities in emergency service accessibility, with significant urban–rural disparities in response coverage and travel times. Rural and peri-urban areas consistently exhibit reduced access to timely emergency care. However, results demonstrate measurable improvements in coverage, routing accuracy, and situational awareness when advanced GIS methods and NG911 datasets are integrated, including enhanced indoor routing and more precise incident location identification (Access to Emergency Care in Rural Illinois; Indoor Routing for School Emergencies). 
The study concludes that geospatial decision support systems play a vital role in improving emergency response efficiency and promoting equity in service provision. Strategic investment in interactive GIS platforms and targeted training can substantially strengthen emergency management outcomes (Designing and Evaluating Interactive Web Maps; Measuring the Impact of Targeted GIS Training).

title: Designing Tailored Training Programs for Diverse Teams

detail.title: Designing Tailored Training Programs for Diverse Teams
detail.abstract: Modern organizations are no longer defined by uniform roles, linear career paths, or homogeneous workforces. Teams today are shaped by diversity across culture, geography, professional background, age, learning preferences, and cognitive styles. At the same time, the pace of technological change continues to compress the lifespan of skills, forcing organizations to rethink how learning happens at scale¹. In this context, traditional, standardized training programs increasingly fail to produce meaningful outcomes. Attendance may be high, but relevance and application often remain low.

title: Barriers to the Formalization of SMEs and Tax Collection Impact

detail.title: Barriers to the Formalization of SMEs and Tax Collection Impact
detail.abstract:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play a pivotal role in economic development, job creation, and the sustainability of national tax systems (Balogun & Rasool, 2024). Despite their significance, many SMEs operate informally, which limits their contribution to government revenue and reduces opportunities for growth. Formalization has been recognized as a critical factor in enhancing tax compliance, promoting transparency, and strengthening fiscal capacity (Chijikwa, 2024; Mehjabeen & Khan, 2024). This study adopts a multi-method approach, including multi-case study analysis, surveys, in-depth interviews with SME owners, and policy document review, to examine the challenges and drivers of SME tax compliance (Rimadhani et al., 2024). Findings indicate that SMEs face significant barriers, including limited awareness of tax obligations, high compliance costs, complex administrative procedures, and insufficient incentives for formalization (Lavic, 2023; Indrianti & Hidayati, 2024). 
The results also reveal that supportive measures, including targeted educational programs, simplified tax processes, and incentive-based formalization initiatives, can significantly improve compliance and expand the tax base. The study underscores the importance of aligning government policies with SME capacities and needs, demonstrating that strategic interventions not only enhance voluntary compliance but also contribute to broader economic development objectives (Mpofu, 2023; Balogun & Rasool, 2024). These insights provide a foundation for policymakers and tax authorities to design effective strategies that encourage SME formalization and optimize revenue generation.

title: Guaranteed Basic Income for Transition-Age Foster Youth: A Policy Review and Economic Rationale

detail.title: Guaranteed Basic Income for Transition-Age Foster Youth: A Policy Review and Economic Rationale
detail.abstract: Transition-age foster youth in the United States face high rates of homelessness, unemployment, and mental health issues. Recently, several Guaranteed Basic Income (GBI) pilot programs have been introduced to address these problems through direct, unconditional cash support. This paper reviews five GBI pilots (2020–2025) that target youth aging out of foster care in California, New York, and Maryland. Using published evaluations, government reports, and nonprofit analyses, we summarize outcomes related to housing stability, employment, education, and mental wellbeing. Although detailed long-term data are still limited, early results indicate that GBI programs lead to noticeable improvements in youth outcomes and can reduce costs for public systems. We examine the economic reasoning for GBI through a social return on investment (SROI) perspective, discuss program features that improve fairness and effectiveness, and highlight opportunities for more thorough research and policy development. These findings present GBI as a powerful policy option deserving of further support and study.

title: Corporate Sustainability under Trade Protectionism: Governance Vulnerability and ESG Reallocation

detail.title: Corporate Sustainability under Trade Protectionism: Governance Vulnerability and ESG Reallocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: Market-based cross-border governance-through trade liberalization, investor scrutiny, and global value chain monitoring-has long played an important role in shaping firms' sustainable development practices. The recent resurgence of trade protectionism raises concerns that these external governance mechanisms may weaken, while policy uncertainty at the institutional level increases. Despite a growing literature on trade-policy uncertainty and firm behavior, evidence remains limited on how firms adjust their sustainability strategies under such regime-level shocks. This study examines firms' sustainability responses to the Section 301 tariffs imposed by the United States on Chinese products during 2018-2019. Exploiting cross-industry variation in tariff exposure and firm-level panel data from Chinese listed companies, the analysis adopts a quasi-experimental framework to explore how protectionist shocks relate to firms' environmental, social, and governance (ESG) engagement. Rather than focusing solely on aggregate ESG outcomes, the study emphasizes potential reallocation across ESG dimensions under heightened uncertainty. The analysis further explores whether differences in domestic policy environments are associated with heterogeneous sustainability responses to trade-policy shocks. By comparing institutional-oriented and market-oriented policy frameworks, the study highlights the role of policy design in shaping firms' sustainability adjustment paths under external uncertainty. Overall, the findings suggest that understanding corporate sustainability under protectionism requires attention not only to overall ESG engagement, but also to its internal composition and institutional context.

title: Housing Capital Gains across the Income Distribution
affiliations: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, Florida International University (FIU) - Hollo School of Real Estate and Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: Housing Capital Gains across the Income Distribution

publicationDetails.journalName: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We show that high-income buyers earn higher capital gains on housing using detailed transaction data from Denmark. Geographic location statistically accounts for nearly all the difference, with little role for aggregate market timing, property type, or other buyer characteristics. This finding is consistent with income-based sorting, whereby higher-income households systematically sort into locations with persistently higher price growth. We test whether credit conditions shape access to locations with higher house-price growth and find no detectable change in buyer composition by income rank around major credit expansions and contractions.

title: Governance Tension Structures in AI-Driven Socio-Technical Systems: An Eight-Dimensional Governance Tension Coordinate Framework within a Multi-Layer Learning Paradigm

detail.title: Governance Tension Structures in AI-Driven Socio-Technical Systems: An Eight-Dimensional Governance Tension Coordinate Framework within a Multi-Layer Learning Paradigm

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence and platform-based technologies are increasingly embedded in global urban–rural digital transformation processes, policymakers face mounting governance challenges in urban–rural digital transformation and AI governance. These challenges can no longer be adequately addressed through conventional policy coordination mechanisms alone. AI-driven platform technologies activate multiple heterogeneous governance constraints operating across different institutional time scales, thereby generating structurally cumulative tensions in decision-making processes. This study addresses a core question in urban–rural digital transformation and AI governance: how can such multidimensional tensions be systematically diagnosed in order to support a human-centred pathway of digital development? Drawing on a multi-layer learning paradigm, the paper proposes an eight-dimensional governance tension coordination framework as a diagnostic tool for analysing how AI-driven socio-technical systems exert simultaneous and irreducible pressures on urban–rural governance. The framework disaggregates governance constraints into eight analytically distinct dimensions and elucidates how these dimensions interact through mechanisms of cross-dimensional coupling. Empirical analysis of platform-driven urban–rural digital transformation in Asian countries demonstrates that digital interventions do not exert uniform effects on existing governance structures. Rather, they selectively activate particular constraint dimensions and generate differentiated patterns of tension through inter-dimensional coupling. This study develops a transferable comparative analytical framework for diagnosing governance tensions across diverse urban–rural socio-technical systems. For urban–rural digital transformation and AI governance, the framework has clear practical value: it enables policymakers to identify, prior to the escalation of conflict, which governance constraints are being activated, how they interact, and along which pathways tensions are likely to propagate. By revealing the structural nature of governance challenges in urban–rural digital contexts, this research contributes to the development of digital transformation pathways that are more resilient, inclusive, and context-sensitive.

title: Predicting Law of Property Act Receivership: Evidence from UK Companies House Charge Data

detail.title: Predicting Law of Property Act Receivership: Evidence from UK Companies House Charge Data
detail.abstract: This study develops and validates a predictive model for Law of Property Act (LPA) receivership appointment using publicly available UK Companies House charge registration data. While existing corporate distress prediction literature focuses predominantly on general insolvency outcomes, secured creditor enforcement through receivership represents a distinct legal and commercial pathway with different predictive characteristics. Analysing 398,750 UK companies with registered charges over a five-year period, we examine whether charge registration patterns, creditor composition, and security structure characteristics can predict subsequent LPA receiver appointments. We classify 510 unique creditor name patterns into 14 categories, enabling granular analysis of creditor type as a predictive feature. Our principal finding is that companies with Qualifying Floating Charge Holders (QFCHs) are 3.5 times more likely to experience receiver appointment than companies with other charge structures (χ² = 1,222, p < 0.0001). This substantially outperforms the model's predictive power for Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL), where the same features yield only 1.25x lift, confirming that receivership and general insolvency represent distinct outcome populations. Secondary findings reveal significant creditor-type effects: companies with challenger bank or specialist buy-to-let lender exposure exhibit 8.4% distress rates, representing 2.95x the baseline. Geographic concentration patterns identify elevated receivership risk in specific regions, with certain postcodes showing distress rates exceeding 15%. These findings have practical implications for secured lenders conducting portfolio stress testing, insolvency practitioners identifying appointment opportunities, and creditors assessing recovery prospects. The methodology demonstrates that charge registration data, freely available from Companies House, contains substantial predictive signal for secured creditor enforcement outcomes that is not captured by conventional credit scoring approaches.

title: SMEs' Perception of Tax Fairness and Its Effect on Compliance

detail.title: SMEs' Perception of Tax Fairness and Its Effect on Compliance
detail.abstract: This study presents a comparative analysis of payroll taxation policies across developed and developing countries, focusing on their design, compliance, and economic implications for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Employing a mixed-method approach, the research integrates an extensive literature review, secondary data analysis, and case study comparisons to examine how different jurisdictions implement and enforce payroll tax regimes. Key findings reveal significant variations in compliance rates, enforcement mechanisms, and the administrative burden placed on SMEs. Developed countries typically exhibit higher levels of automation, transparency, and taxpayer support, resulting in improved compliance and lower administrative costs. In contrast, developing countries often face challenges related to limited administrative capacity, weaker enforcement, and lower taxpayer awareness, which collectively hinder effective tax collection and compliance. The study underscores that the effectiveness of payroll tax systems is not solely determined by statutory rates but heavily relies on robust administration, transparent procedures, and continuous taxpayer education. These insights suggest that policy reforms aimed at strengthening institutional capacity, simplifying tax processes, and enhancing awareness programs can improve compliance and reduce economic distortions, particularly for SMEs. The findings contribute to the broader understanding of payroll taxation as a critical component of fiscal policy and provide guidance for governments seeking to optimize tax collection while supporting business growth.

title:
Design Implications of Foundation Depth Theory: 
Exit Architecture and Legitimation Dynamics

detail.title:
Design Implications of Foundation Depth Theory: 
Exit Architecture and Legitimation Dynamics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
