detail.abstract: Contemporary models of human behavior frequently isolate cognition, behavior, and identity into separate analytical domains. Psychology emphasizes thought and emotion, organizational theory prioritizes performance and outcomes, and security or justice frameworks focus on control and compliance. While each approach captures part of the human experience, this fragmentation obscures the deeper structure through which human agency operates. This paper introduces and integrates three original frameworks: the Identity-Value-Purpose-Design (IVPD) framework, which describes the ontological structure of the human person; the Infinite Loop Thinking Framework (ILTF), which models cognition as a recursive perception-interpretation-action system; and the Goal-Interpretation-Obstruction-Conflict (GIOC) framework, which explains how internal meaning-making manifests as cooperation or conflict in the external world. The central thesis is that human agency operates as a vertical cascade: identity structures cognition, cognition governs interpretation, and interpretation determines behavioral response to obstruction. When identity is intrinsically grounded, cognition remains coherent and conflict is navigated constructively. When identity is extrinsically contingent, cognition collapses into survival loops and conflict escalates disproportionately. By synthesizing these frameworks into a unified model, this paper offers a practical and predictive architecture for understanding leadership failure, psychological stagnation, institutional dysfunction, and violent conflict. The model provides a basis for early intervention, de-escalation, and sustainable human development across disciplines.

title: The Innovation Tax: Generative AI Adoption, Productivity Paradox, and Systemic Risk in the U.S. Banking Sector

detail.title: The Innovation Tax: Generative AI Adoption, Productivity Paradox, and Systemic Risk in the U.S. Banking Sector
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the causal impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) adoption on productivity and systemic risk in the U.S. banking sector. Using a novel dataset linking SEC 10-Q filings to Federal Reserve regulatory data for 809 financial institutions over 2018--2025, we employ two complementary identification strategies: Dynamic Spatial Durbin Models (DSDM) to capture network spillovers and Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) for causal inference using the November 2022 ChatGPT release as an exogenous shock. Our findings reveal a striking ``Productivity Paradox'': while DSDM estimates show that AI-adopting banks are high performers ($\beta > 0$), the causal SDID analysis documents a significant ``Implementation Tax''---adopting banks experience a 428-basis-point decline in ROE as they absorb GenAI integration costs. This tax falls disproportionately on smaller institutions, with bottom-quartile banks suffering a 517-basis-point ROE decline compared to 129 basis points for larger banks, suggesting that economies of scale provide significant advantages in AI implementation. Most critically, our DSDM analysis reveals significant positive spillovers ($\theta = 0.161$ for ROA, $p < 0.01$; $\theta = 0.679$ for ROE, $p < 0.05$), with spillovers among large banks reaching $\theta = 3.13$ for ROE, indicating that the U.S. banking system is becoming ``algorithmically coupled.'' This synchronization of AI-driven decision-making creates a new channel for systemic contagion: a technical failure in widely-adopted AI models could trigger correlated shocks across the entire financial network.

detail.abstract:
Modern institutions increasingly rely on intelligence systems to influence judgment, prioritization, eligibility, supervision, and enforcement. While constitutional and governance frameworks define the conditions under which institutional intelligence may exist, institutional failure most often arises at the point of reliance rather than at the level of system design or technical performance.

This paper introduces Sovereign Intelligence Stewardship (SIS) as a non-binding, jurisdiction-neutral interpretive constitutional instrument governing the legitimacy of institutional reliance on intelligence. SIS operates within a closed constitutional corpus alongside rather than prescribing implementation controls or governance templates, SIS formalizes a set of stewardship axes—authority, reliance, accountability, contestability, continuity, and sovereignty—through which institutions must interpret whether reliance on intelligence preserves constitutional legitimacy under their own mandates.

By rejecting one-size-fits-all standards, certification schemes, and checklist-based governance, SIS positions institutional judgment, rather than technical compliance, as the primary safeguard of legitimacy under scale, change, and delegation. The paper is intended for policymakers, regulators, and institutional leaders concerned with the constitutional governance of intelligence in high-authority environments.

title: Prefatory Observations on Venezuela: A Brief Analysis

detail.title: Prefatory Observations on Venezuela: A Brief Analysis
detail.abstract: When I look at the recent United States strike on Venezuela and the forcible transfer of Nicolás Maduro to US custody, I cannot see it in simple “right versus wrong” terms. Procedurally it collides with the very principles of international law, at the same time, on the streets of Venezuela there is also visible relief and hope at the prospect of political change after the fall of Nicolás Maduro’s regime. From where I sit as an observer of international politics, I start from the legal side because that is where the operation is at its weakest. Under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, states must refrain from the use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state, except in self‑defence or with Security Council authorisation. In the Venezuelan case, there was no UN mandate, and Venezuela had not launched an “armed attack” on the United States that could justify unilateral self‑defence under Article 51.

Steenstra (2025) presented Governance Genetic Engineering (GGE) framework explaining
healthcare transformation failure through governance autoimmunity triggered by stakeholder
proliferation, objective misalignment, and governance monopoly. Subsequent cross-domain
analysis revealed GGE instantiates a universal principle operating across biological,
organizational, digital, and governmental substrates.
This paper articulates Complex System Immunity Theory (CSIT): any information-processing
system protecting itself from threats under uncertainty will converge on identical defensive
architecture through computational necessity. This architecture has intrinsic pathological failure
mode—autoimmunity—where protective mechanisms evolve toward crude blocking of
beneficial inputs alongside genuine threats through Darwinian selection favouring efficiency
over accuracy.
Structural isomorphism between biological immune systems (Type 1 diabetes, lupus) and
organizational governance (NHS transformation failure, corporate innovation death, academic
paradigm calcification, platform moderation dysfunction) demonstrates mathematical identity,
not metaphorical analogy. Historical trajectory (NHS innovation ‘by passable’ 1980s,
‘impossible’ 2020s) validates crude evolution predictions. Cross-sector comparison (automotive
success vs. healthcare failure with identical stakeholder counts) validates alignment hypothesis.
CSIT generates falsifiable predictions testable through natural experiments: nascent systems
(Uganda healthcare, 2026-2028) will/won't maintain innovation capacity through governance
immunity engineering; established systems (NHS) will/won't reverse learned crudeness through
intervention. Prevention-intervention economic differential predicted to exceed 40:1 (£2-4M vs.
£200M+), consistent with change management failure rates documented over 40 years (Kotter,
1995; Beer & Nohria, 2000).
CSIT provides theoretical foundation underlying GGE while demonstrating broader applicability
across any domain exhibiting stakeholder proliferation with objective misalignment under
monopolistic governance.
This paper is intended as a theory-building working paper to establish priority and invite critique;
formal mathematical specification and large-scale empirical testing are ongoing.

title: Dynamic Normative Feedback Model: Organising Ethical Feedback Systems in Knowledge-based Teams
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dynamic Normative Feedback Model: Organising Ethical Feedback Systems in Knowledge-based Teams
detail.abstract:
In knowledge-based organisations, top-down feedback has a significant influence on the entire organisation’s culture and efficiency. However, many existing theories lack a full-process system that provides clear methods for managers to deliver both efficient and ethical feedback. This thesis investigates how lower-level management in Dutch for-profit companies can transform top-down feedback into more ethical feedback while minimising efficiency trade-offs. 

 

The thesis forms the foundation of the DNFM through a mixed-methods design comprising a survey with 199 respondents, 108 employee stakeholder narratives, 15 participants in an exploratory experiment, and multiple expert interviews. 

 

Key findings reveal that feedback is perceived as most ethical when it is developmental at its core rather than evaluative, concrete,  clear, and fair. Across multiple methods, the same result emerges: feedback from a virtue-ethical transformational manager is considered the best, based on moral norms, with important concepts such as psychological safety and ownership. These concepts are checked and compared with the literature. Statistical analysis showed that quality and ethics correlated strongly, highlighting the importance of developing substance and supporting the need for profound changes in communication.

 

By integrating leadership theories, metaethical-to-normative frameworks, applied psychology, and business theories with newly discovered insights, the DNFM is proposed. The model emphasises flexibility, actionability, managerial duties, and continuous ethical calibration. Practical recommendations and actionable plans are formulated for Dutch knowledge-based teams. The Dynamic Normative Feedback Model (DNFM) fills the research gap by adopting a distinct approach to current Dutch practices. It provides a broader framework, especially when it comes to ethical demands and integrating multidisciplinary approaches.

 

This profielwerkstuk shows that ethical feedback can not only have minimal trade-offs for efficiency but can even increase long-term performance in the 21st century.

title: The State-Substituted Social Enterprise: Fused Governance and Rational Decoupling in Elite Thai Secondary Education

detail.title: The State-Substituted Social Enterprise: Fused Governance and Rational Decoupling in Elite Thai Secondary Education
detail.abstract: Collaborative governance theory conventionally presumes a durable functional demarcation between state agencies and non-state stakeholders (Ansell & Gash, 2008). This article contests this boundary-centric assumption through an empirical study of elite Thai public secondary schools that deliver world-class outcomes despite chronic state fiscal fragility. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design (𝑁 = 487 stakeholders; 66 interviews), we reconceptualize these institutions as State-Substituted Social Enterprises (SSEs). Quantitative analysis confirms a state of Structural Fusion, wherein stakeholder engagement and governance are empirically isomorphic (CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000). We identify a "Shadow Balance Sheet"-a parallel financial ecosystem where network funding systematically substitutes for state provision-and "Rational Decoupling," where governance strategically aligns with market-valued quality while statistically rejecting state-mandated "Zombie Metrics" (𝛽 =-.08, 𝑝 = .153). We conclude that in environments of institutional fragility, the logical endpoint of collaboration is not partnership, but the functional displacement of the state by a fused, stakeholder-led sovereign unit.

title: Clarification of on-site Adaptivity and Hybrid Complex-Modular Characteristics

detail.title: Clarification of on-site Adaptivity and Hybrid Complex-Modular Characteristics
detail.abstract: To enhance the rigor and academic value of the concept of On-site Adaptive Innovation, it is essential to provide clear definitions and structured explanations of the core terms: On-site Adaptivity and Hybrid Complex-Modular Characteristics. These two elements constitute the distinctive foundation that differentiates this concept from existing notions such as architectural innovation or disruptive innovation.

title: Beyond the Paper Shield: A Real Analysis of the DOJ Compliance Program and the Similar Provision in Law 12.846/13 regarding Fraud in Large Public Infrastructure Works

detail.title: Beyond the Paper Shield: A Real Analysis of the DOJ Compliance Program and the Similar Provision in Law 12.846/13 regarding Fraud in Large Public Infrastructure Works
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the intersection between the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) "Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs" (ECCP) and Brazil's Anti-Corruption Law (Law 12.846/13), specifically within the context of public infrastructure fraud. The author argues that Brazil's regime of strict liability (responsabilidade objetiva) imposes a harsher burden than the U.S. FCPA's "willful violation" standard. The paper challenges the "Paper Shield" of bureaucratic compliance-where glossy manuals fail to reach remote construction sites-and proposes utilizing Brazil's rigorous system of "Clearance Certificates" (Certidões Negativas) as an automated control mechanism that effectively satisfies both DOJ effectiveness standards and Brazilian due diligence requirements.

title: The Metacognitive Paradox of AI-Assisted Creativity: A Theoretical Extension

detail.title: The Metacognitive Paradox of AI-Assisted Creativity: A Theoretical Extension
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into organizational workflows raises fundamental questions about the long-term effects of AI assistance on human creative capabilities. This article provides a comprehensive theoretical extension of Sun et al.'s (2025) field experiment, which demonstrated that LLM assistance enhances creative output during use but diminishes subsequent independent creativity-particularly for individuals with lower metacognitive ability. We develop the metacognitive paradox framework to explain this phenomenon: AI tools designed to augment human creativity may inadvertently suppress the very cognitive processes that sustain independent creative capacity. Drawing on metacognition theory, cognitive offloading research, automation and human factors literatures, and the componential model of creativity, we articulate the mechanisms through which LLM assistance affects creative cognition, specify temporal dynamics and boundary conditions, and generate testable propositions for future research. We explicitly compare our framework against alternative theoretical explanationsincluding cognitive load theory, motivational accounts, and expertise development perspectives-and provide methodological guidance for testing our propositions. Our analysis reveals that the relationship between AI assistance and human creativity is neither uniformly beneficial nor detrimental but contingent upon individual metacognitive capabilities, patterns of tool use, task characteristics, and organizational context. We conclude with implications for theory, research methodology, organizational practice, and the ethical dimensions of AI-augmented work.

title: Coordination of Competitive Robots and Workers in On-Demand Logistics Services: Filling in "the Price of Equity"
affiliations: Department of Data and Systems Engineering, The University of Hong Kong and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Coordination of Competitive Robots and Workers in On-Demand Logistics Services: Filling in "the Price of Equity"
detail.abstract: The rapid rise of robotic technologies poses an existential threat to human workers in on-demand logistics services, potentially displacing millions in ride-hailing and delivery. In platforms with all-human workforces, we identify a notable inefficiency⎯the "price of equity" (POE)⎯stemming from indiscriminate order dispatching that disregards differences in order profitability. Robot threats can be resolved along with the POE if the platform adopts a threshold matching strategy, deploying robots to less profitable orders with congestion and reserving workers for more valuable assignments. To explore this potential, we develop an analytical model to estimate the POE by comparing all-inclusive with selective order admission based on profitability. Real-world data reveal a maximum potential loss of 24% in revenue during demand peaks. Motivated by this inefficiency, we derive the threshold matching strategy for platforms managing both human workers and robots, while ensuring uniform service levels for customers. With an appropriate number of robots, the POE in workers' earnings can be fully restored. Regarding robot fleet decisions of strategic platforms under public regulations in the transition stage, relative to the maximum allowable fleet mandating no harm to workers, platforms deem robot adoption profitable only when technology is sufficiently mature (unit robot costs are sufficiently low). Through a cross-period coordination scheme combined with a subsidy that taxes part of workers' surplus from robotaxi adoption to fund robot procurement, the maximum coordinating robot procurement cost for socially beneficial adoption doubles from approximately 150 to 300 thousand CNY per vehicle, advancing robot introduction before 2030.

title:
The Separation Decision Stack 
Why Early Choices Shape Divestiture Outcomes Long Before Day One

detail.title:
The Separation Decision Stack 
Why Early Choices Shape Divestiture Outcomes Long Before Day One
detail.abstract: In complex divestitures, execution issues are often treated as the primary source of value leakage. Based on practical experience, many of these issues originate much earlier, when foundational separation decisions are left implicit or postponed until buyer preferences are fully known. By the time execution begins, teams are already constrained by assumptions that were never explicitly aligned. This paper presents the Separation Decision Stack, a practitioner-developed framework that highlights fourteen early decisions that anchor separation planning and materially influence downstream outcomes across systems, people, contracts, and transition services. The paper is written for transaction leaders, investors, and operators focused on reducing execution risk and preserving value in large-scale divestitures.

title: The Impact of a National Transition of Treatment Platform on the Acceptance of Internet-Delivered Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: A Longitudinal Study Among Norwegian Therapists
affiliations: University of Bergen, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Amsterdam and University of Bergen - Haukeland University Hospital

detail.title: The Impact of a National Transition of Treatment Platform on the Acceptance of Internet-Delivered Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: A Longitudinal Study Among Norwegian Therapists
detail.abstract: Background:Therapists’ acceptance of internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) is critical for successful and sustained implementation. However, little is known about how acceptance is affected by changes in delivery platforms.Objective:To investigate how therapists’ acceptance of iCBT changes during a national transition to a new delivery platform. Methods:During a national change in delivery platform, 46 therapists (69% of the national population; N = 67) providing iCBT in Norwegian specialist health services, completed questionnaires at five time points over 18 months. The study applied an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) which accounted for both patient and therapists as users of iCBT. Measures included TAM constructs, individual characteristics and place of employment. Multilevel models assessed changes in acceptance over time and baseline variance at therapist and organizational levels.Results:Overall acceptance of iCBT was high at baseline and remained largely stable throughout the transition. Therapist perception of patients’ ease of use increased significantly over time and was clearly distinguished from their perception of their own user experience. Notably, therapists’ acceptance of the new platform was high even before they had gained hands-on user experience.Conclusion:Among experienced iCBT therapists’, acceptance appears resilient to disruptions caused by changes in treatment platforms. Acceptance of a new platform is not dependent on positive user experience alone and may be affected by efforts that influence therapists’ expectations prior to implementation. Therapists’ perceptions of their patients’ user experience are likely important for their acceptance but remain poorly understood.

title: Structural Coherence and Rupture Physics: Part 2 -Cross-Institutional and Cross-Domain Validation of the SCFL Operator

detail.title: Structural Coherence and Rupture Physics: Part 2 -Cross-Institutional and Cross-Domain Validation of the SCFL Operator

detail.abstract: This paper presents the first cross-institutional and cross-domain empirical validation of a physics-grade coherence measurement-the SCFL (Structural Coherence and Failure Linearity) operator-capable of detecting rupture months before external indicators across financial, organizational, and human-system environments. Using Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), Signature Bank, and First Republic Bank as primary case studies, we demonstrate that all three institutions exhibited the same invariant coherence signature: a transition through a 2% coherence regime boundary, followed by a deterministic monotonic decay and a measurable rupture horizon. For SVB, this horizon extended approximately seven months prior to collapse, during which external solvency indicators remained stable and supervisory tools failed to detect instability. We further show that the same coherence signature appears in non-financial systems, including organizational metadata (Glassdoor temporal variance), healthcare staffing and burnout datasets, and community-level human-system signals. These cross-domain validations demonstrate that coherence behaves as a universal structural quantity rather than a domain-specific metric. The SCFL operator is shown to be reproducible, falsifiable, and domain-agnostic, satisfying the criteria for a scientific measurement substrate. The 2023 banking cascade produced ripple impacts exceeding $400 billion, including Deposit Insurance Fund depletion, emergency liquidity facilities, market value destruction, and real-economy credit tightening. In contrast, coherence-based early detection identified intervention windows costing less than $15 billion across all three institutions. This establishes a 20:1 to 60:1 economic advantage for coherence-based intervention and demonstrates the inadequacy of traditional solvency tools, which measure state rather than structural stability. The findings of this paper establish coherence measurement as a new actuarial substrate and a universal scientific law governing human-system stability. The SCFL operator provides a reproducible, physics-grade framework for early rupture detection, cross-domain risk assessment, and systemic resilience modeling, with implications for finance, healthcare, organizational governance, and public policy

title: Variance Collapse as a Leading Indicator of Institutional Failure: Evidence from the Enron Email Corpus

detail.title: Variance Collapse as a Leading Indicator of Institutional Failure: Evidence from the Enron Email Corpus

declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract: Catastrophic organizational failures are a dominant source of tail risk in professional liability, directors' and officers' insurance, employment practices liability, and related lines. Existing actuarial treatments model such events as rare stochastic realizations, largely because no stable early-warning observable has been available prior to loss attachment. This paper introduces a non-interpretive, physics-grade measurement framework that detects deterministic organizational decay under sustained load. Using the publicly available Enron email corpus with fixed historical ground truth, we demonstrate that organizational rupture is preceded by a measurable decay regime characterized by persistent negative drift, variance collapse, cohort-level propagation, and a bounded rupture horizon. These signals emerge approximately six to nine months prior to observable failure, with variance on the order of ±2%, compared to ±12% typical of narrativelayer approaches. The existence of such an observable materially alters actuarial loss distributions by enabling stage-based risk classification, pre-attachment repricing, and exposure exit, thereby truncating catastrophic tail risk without requiring precise event timing or guaranteed intervention success.

title: Marine Greens in Ocean-Based Climate Adaptation and Resilience Building

detail.title: Marine Greens in Ocean-Based Climate Adaptation and Resilience Building
detail.abstract: Climate change poses profound threats to ocean and coastal systems through rising sea levels, ocean warming, acidification, and increased frequency of extreme weather events. These impacts undermine ecosystem stability, coastal livelihoods, and global food security. Marine greens-encompassing seagrasses, macroalgae (seaweeds), and microalgae-have emerged as vital components of ocean-based climate adaptation and resilience-building strategies. Beyond their recognized role in carbon sequestration, marine greens provide critical ecosystem services that enhance ecological resilience, protect coastlines, and support socioeconomic adaptation. This review examines the role of marine greens in climate adaptation and resilience building, focusing on their ecological functions, mechanisms of resilience enhancement, and applications in coastal protection, food systems, and community livelihoods. The paper also discusses environmental, economic, and social benefits, alongside scientific, technical, and governance challenges. Case studies from different regions illustrate practical applications and lessons learned. The review concludes by highlighting future research directions and policy pathways necessary to integrate marine greens into comprehensive ocean-based climate adaptation frameworks. Harnessing the full potential of marine greens offers a nature-based, cost-effective, and multifunctional approach to building resilient coastal and marine systems in a changing climate.

title: Religion as an Economic Institution in Sub-Saharan Africa

detail.abstract: Religion occupies a central position in the social, political, and cultural life of Sub-Saharan Africa. While existing scholarship has examined its moral authority, social capital, and political influence, its economic role remains marginal in mainstream development analysis. This paper reconceptualises religious institutions as economic institutions that mobilise resources, accumulate capital, shape labour relations, and influence household and national development outcomes. Drawing on political economy and institutional economics, the study introduces the Religious Economic Complex (REC) framework, which explains how faith, trust, and cultural legitimacy are transformed into sustained economic power. Using a mixed-methods approach combining household survey data (N ≈ 45,000), crosscountry development indicators, and qualitative case studies from Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa, the paper demonstrates that religious institutions operate as quasi-market actors largely outside formal regulatory oversight. The findings indicate that religious economic activity is associated with significant opportunity costs for households and is linked to long-term development trajectories, particularly industrialisation and productive investment. By repositioning religion at the centre of economic analysis, the paper contributes a novel institutional perspective to development studies and highlights the importance of incorporating religious economic activity into development frameworks.

title: Coastal Ecosystem Restoration Using Marine Greens as a Climate Strategy

detail.title: Coastal Ecosystem Restoration Using Marine Greens as a Climate Strategy
detail.abstract: Coastal ecosystems are among the most productive and valuable environments on Earth, yet they are increasingly threatened by climate change, pollution, and unsustainable human activities. Marine greens-including seagrasses, macroalgae, and microalgae-play a critical role in coastal ecosystem functioning and offer significant potential as nature-based solutions for climate change mitigation and adaptation. This review examines the use of marine greens in coastal ecosystem restoration as a strategic climate intervention. It explores the ecological characteristics of marine greens, their role in carbon sequestration and blue carbon storage, and their capacity to enhance ecosystem resilience. The paper discusses restoration approaches, climate mitigation pathways, socioeconomic benefits, and policy relevance, alongside challenges related to scientific uncertainty, governance, and environmental risks. Case studies from different global regions are reviewed to highlight successful applications and best practices. The study concludes that restoring coastal ecosystems using marine greens represents a cost-effective, multifunctional, and sustainable climate strategy that aligns environmental conservation with socioeconomic development, provided that restoration efforts are supported by robust science, inclusive governance, and long-term investment.

title: Reorienting the Research Onion: A Triadic Moral Foundation for Ethical Inquiry in Built Environment Research

detail.title: Reorienting the Research Onion: A Triadic Moral Foundation for Ethical Inquiry in Built Environment Research
detail.abstract:
Built environment research-particularly in construction management-has increasingly reduced research philosophy to a perfunctory compliance exercise, inserting formulaic definitions into methodology chapters while obscuring ethical responsibility and the lived realities of marginalized actors in the contract chain. This detachment perpetuates the Sophist Trap: performative academic ritual over genuine moral purpose. 
This paper reconstructs the philosophical triad of ontology, epistemology, and axiology (OEA) as the moral foundation of inquiry. It introduces Shèn Dú (慎獨, vigilance in solitude)-a core Confucian discipline of maintaining unwavering moral integrity even when unobserved-as the proactive self-cultivation practice that ensures triadic coherence. Drawing on classical Confucian texts, Neo-Confucian thought, and decades of fieldwork across Southeast Asian construction sites, the paper explores Shèn Dú's affinities with Kantian deontology (internal duty, autonomy, and unconditional dignity) while highlighting its relational, context-sensitive, and practice-based strengths. 
The analysis revises Saunders' Research Onion by placing axiology as the outermost layer-making values the primary driver of methodological choices-while drawing inspiration from Creswell's transformative worldview to prioritize epistemic justice, human dignity, and action-oriented change. Vignettes and interpretive contrasts illustrate how philosophical stances shape divergent readings of empirical events. The paper concludes with practical implications for research design, assessment, and dissemination that demand vigilance in solitude and truly transformative inquiry.

title: Household Reliance on Artificial Intelligence for Financial Advice: Evidence from the United States
affiliations: , Texas Tech University and Missouri Southern State University - Plaster School of Business

detail.title: Household Reliance on Artificial Intelligence for Financial Advice: Evidence from the United States
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first micro-level evidence from a nationally representative U.S. household survey on individuals' reliance on artificial intelligence for financial advice. Using weighted binomial logit models, we examine how digital readiness, risk preferences, investment sophistication, and behavioral frictions shape AI advice adoption. Mobile banking usage and risk tolerance significantly increase reliance on AI advice, while ownership of securities and cryptocurrencies reduces it. Behavioral factors-financial anxiety, time burden, and perceived financial constraint-emerge as the strongest and most robust predictors. The results indicate that AI financial advice primarily functions as a behavioral and cognitive support technology rather than a substitute for financial expertise, with important implications for financial inclusion and consumer protection.

title: Education Crises in Protracted Conflicts: A Comparative Analysis of African and Middle Eastern Contexts

detail.abstract: This research paper analyzes the different patterns of education system collapse in protracted armed conflicts through a systematic comparison between selected countries from Sub-Saharan Africa (Nigeria, Ethiopia, Sudan) and the Middle East (Yemen, Syria). The study employs a comparative case study methodology and analyzes secondary data from peerreviewed academic sources and international reports. The results reveal fundamental differences in educational collapse patterns between the two regions: while African cases are characterized by a structural learning quality crisis exacerbated by conflict, Middle Eastern cases tend toward patterns of central institutional collapse or competitive fragmentation of the education system. The paper concludes that recovery responses must be differentiated, emphasizing pedagogical reforms in African contexts and complex political-diplomatic mechanisms in Middle Eastern contexts.

title: A Unified Research Program and Pre-Registration of Terminal and Irreversible Honor Capital (Non-Equivalence, Dynamic Foundations, and Institutional Boundary Conditions)

detail.title: A Unified Research Program and Pre-Registration of Terminal and Irreversible Honor Capital (Non-Equivalence, Dynamic Foundations, and Institutional Boundary Conditions)
detail.abstract: This paper provides a unified and formal foundation for Honor Economics, a theoretical framework in which honor enters utility as a terminal, posthumously determined, and irreversible component. Building on prior conceptual and dynamic formulations (Higuchi, 2026a; 2026b), the paper consolidates definitions, establishes a rigorous non-representability (non-equivalence) theorem, and fixes the analytical boundaries of a four-module research program. Honor is defined by strict boundary conditions: (i) posthumous determination, (ii) irreversibility once fixed, (iii) social recording based exclusively on cumulative public monetary contributions, and (iv) the absence of material rewards, legal privileges, or titles. Under these conditions, honor enters lifetime welfare only through a terminal value. The core result shows that no contemporaneous, time-additive utility formulation can replicate terminal honor, even when honor accumulation is monotone and irreversible. Using a continuous-time dynamic optimization model, the paper demonstrates that terminal honor generates shadow-value conditions that have no analogue in warm-glow, reputation, or signaling models. When honor accumulation is 2 nonlinear and convex beyond a threshold, rational agents may optimally choose extreme and highly concentrated public contributions. This paper does not present new empirical results or policy prescriptions. Instead, it functions as a formal pre-registration of the Honor Economics research program, fixing its conceptual scope, canonical models, and testable restrictions prior to further theoretical or empirical development.

title: Sovereignty and Speech: The Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme and the Implied Freedom of Political Communication

detail.title: Sovereignty and Speech: The Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme and the Implied Freedom of Political Communication
detail.abstract: Owing to recent allegations of coordinated foreign interference operations designed to erode the integrity of elections and other democratic processes across the world, the exposure and regulation of foreign political influence in the domestic space has become a significant point of concern in national security discourse. In 2017, the Commonwealth Government proposed a swathe of legislation aimed towards addressing the burgeoning issue of foreign interference in Australian politics. Included within this legislative package was the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Act 2018 (Cth), a statutory instrument that provided for the creation of a public database upon which individuals undertaking political activities in Australia on behalf of a foreign government or organisation would be required to register. This thesis contends that although there is a clear and present need to address uncontrolled foreign disinformation and interference campaigns, the FITS Act, in both its conceptual operation and practice, is not fit for purpose in combating the issue and, in unjustifiably burdening the implied freedom of political communication, causes more harm to democratic institutions in Australia than its proposed benefits. Through the use of a combined doctrinal and comparative methodology, this thesis assesses the practical shortcomings and constitutional deficiencies of the FITS Act and situates it within the wider discussion of international policy responses to the issue of covert foreign influence, particularly with reference to its legislative predecessor in the United States’ Foreign Agent Registration Act. This thesis also suggests that the future of the implied freedom of political communication is in jeopardy in Australia, referencing emerging High Court jurisprudence, and will propose potential avenues of reform to both address doctrinal concerns of the FITS Act and to ensure the protection and possible expansion of constitutional speech protections.

title: Detecting Silent Governance Failure: Semantic Entropy, Dissent Exhaustion, and Circuit Breakers

detail.title: Detecting Silent Governance Failure: Semantic Entropy, Dissent Exhaustion, and Circuit Breakers

detail.abstract: Current AI governance focuses on the noise of failure—errors, bias, and misuse. However, in high-stakes bureaucracies, the most catastrophic failures manifest as silence. We introduce Resolution Collapse: a condition in which human oversight persists as a procedural ritual, as organizational efficiency smooths away the friction required to distinguish routine cases from exceptions. To address this, we shift the focus from error prevention to failure legibility. We propose Governance Drift Indicators (GDIs) to detect the semantic and temporal erosion of judgment before it becomes epistemically irreversible. Furthermore, we argue that when oversight collapses, “soft” interventions such as retraining are insufficient. Instead, we introduce a circuit breaker architecture: a structural mechanism designed to halt or isolate AI-assisted processes when epistemic capacity is lost. Finally, we define the concept of a Proper Ending—a controlled termination that preserves institutional memory. These contributions reframe AI governance not as the pursuit of uninterrupted operation, but as the capacity to stop systems transparently and responsibly.

title: Design and Performance Optimization of a Multi-Purpose Autonomous Rover for Planetary and Terrestrial Applications
affiliations: , , , , , , , ,  and Department of Mechanical Engineering, Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology

detail.title: Design and Performance Optimization of a Multi-Purpose Autonomous Rover for Planetary and Terrestrial Applications
detail.abstract: Autonomous rovers are essential for space exploration and terrestrial applications, including search and rescue, surveillance, and industrial inspection. This paper presents Prochesta V3.0, a cost-effective modular autonomous rover platform that demonstrates significant technological advancement while maintaining economic accessibility for developing nations. The rover achieves a 30.7% mass reduction compared to its predecessor while enhancing scientific capabilities through modular architecture, prioritizing weight optimization and operational versatility. Key technical achievements include a four-wheel bar-differential suspension system enabling obstacle traversal up to twice the wheel diameter, a five-degree-of-freedom robotic arm with 5 kg payload capacity, and advanced scientific analysis capabilities featuring 30 cm drilling depth and threefold sample storage capacity. Enhanced vision systems utilizing Zed 2 cameras provide double the detection range and 54% wider field of view compared to previous configurations, enabling superior autonomous navigation. The communication system achieves 5 km line-of-sight range with industrial-grade reliability. Comprehensive field testing validates performance across diverse terrain conditions, including rocky surfaces, sandy substrates, and structural debris. At $3,800 USD compared to commercial alternatives exceeding $10,000 USD, Prochesta V3.0 offers compelling economic advantages while supporting applications spanning space exploration, emergency response, defense operations, and industrial inspection. This work demonstrates developing nations' capability to achieve world-class engineering solutions through innovative resource-efficient design approaches.

title: National Innovation Capabilty Enablers and Outcomes, Corruption, and Progression to Higher Stages of CBDC Adoption

detail.title: National Innovation Capabilty Enablers and Outcomes, Corruption, and Progression to Higher Stages of CBDC Adoption
detail.abstract: Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) have garnered much interest from scholars, practitioners, and policymakers alike. A survey of the literature that has explored a country's characteristics as determinants of its CBDC adoption suggests a multifaceted landscape shaped by a confluence of political, legal, economic, financial, technological, social, and cultural factors. However, less is known about the role that the national system of innovation (NSI) characteristics may play in the adoption of a CBDC. To fill this research gap, this dissertation explored how five national innovation capability enablers (i.e., institutions, human research and capital, infrastructure, market sophistication, and business sophistication) and two national innovation capability outcomes (i.e., knowledge and technology outputs and creative outputs) influenced a country's advancement to higher stages of CBDC adoption. Further, it examined the role that corruption--defined as the abuse of entrusted power (or public office) for private gain--played as a moderator, i.e., whether it strengthened or weakened the impact of the five national innovation enablers and the two national innovation outcomes on a country's progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption, respectively. Analyzing a unique dataset compiling archival data gathered from the CBDC Tracker, Global Innovation Index, Global Governance Indicators, Corruption Perceptions Index, and Worldwide Corruption Index by employing ordered logistic regression, the study in this dissertation found that none of the five national innovation capability enablers--institutions, human capital and research, infrastructure, market sophistication, and business sophistication--had statistically significant positive impact on a country's progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption. However, creative outputs--one of the two national innovation capability outcomes--were found to have statistically significant positive impact on a country's progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption, while the other national innovation capability outcomes (i.e., knowledge and technology outputs) did not. Further, corruption was found to play a moderating role in the case of two national innovation capability enablers. Corruption positively moderated the relationship between institutions and a country's progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption, whereas corruption negatively moderated the relationship between market sophistication and a country's progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption. In other words, the positive relationship between institutions and a country's progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption was stronger in countries with lower levels of corruption than in those with higher levels of corruption, whereas the positive relationship between market sophistication and a country's progression to higher stages of CBDC adoption was stronger in countries with higher levels of corruption than in those with lower levels of corruption.

title: Impact of FDI on Economic Growth: An Empirical Evidence from Bangladesh

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the impact of foreign direct investment (FDI) on
economic growth (GDP per capita) of Bangladesh using time series data from 1991 to
2021. Autoregressive distributed lagged (ARDL) approach is applied to capture both
short-run and long-run relationships among the variables under consideration. The
Granger causality test is also employed to check the causality between the variables.
The findings show that FDI has a significant negative impact on economic growth of
Bangladesh in the short-run, but FDI’s contribution to economic growth of Bangladesh
is insignificant in the long-run. Only Human capital formation determines the economic
growth of Bangladesh in the long-run, which indicates that impact of FDI on economic
growth is rather indirect.
Furthermore, the granger causality test finds no evidence of causality between FDI and
economic growth of Bangladesh. It seems that Bangladesh hasn’t, so far, succeeded to
attract sufficient amount of FDI inflows to make a positive & significant impact
(contribution) on (to) the economy.

title: Health Co-benefits of Net-Zero Pathways vs. Transition Costs: A Literature Review
affiliations: University Grenoble Alpes, Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers (CNAM), Students, , Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers (CNAM), Students and University Grenoble Alpes

detail.title: Health Co-benefits of Net-Zero Pathways vs. Transition Costs: A Literature Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a systematic literature review and did not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This work benefited from funding provided by the French government, managed by the National Research Agency (ANR) under the France 2030 program, reference ANR-25-EXTR-0009.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. No clinical trial was conducted.

detail.abstract: Net-zero pathways will generate substantial health co-benefits, which are often large, spatially concentrated, and realized in the near term. Since these features can substantially strengthen the case for ambitious mitigation, it is necessary to quantify these co-benefits and compare them across policy options within a cost-benefit analysis. Yet no previous work has systematically synthesised the methods and outcomes used in this literature to support robust and comparable policy conclusions. We systematically identify seventeen original studies that report monetized health benefits alongside transition costs for forward-looking 2 °C or net-zero scenarios. We extract comparable quantitative indicators (principally benefit-cost ratios) and document key modeling choices. Two main results emerge: first, all studies focus on health benefits arising from reductions in air pollution, while health benefits from active mobility and dietary change are largely not covered; second, with the exception of two Europe-focused studies, all conclude that, under a 2 °C-consistent pathway, health benefits exceed transition costs. Despite this convergence, substantial differences in analytical scope, temporal horizons, and valuation methods limit comparability and weaken the existing evidence. We therefore provide the first comprehensive overview of the underlying modeling approaches and show how these choices shape cost-benefit analysis outcomes. Finally, we propose targeted recommendations to strengthen scientific robustness and policy relevance, including improving comparability across studies, increasing regional analyses, reporting both tangible and intangible costs and benefits in a temporally explicit manner.

title: Economic and Environmental Feasibility of Renewable Energy Integrated Grid for Charging Three-Wheeler Electric Vehicles in Dhaka City

detail.title: Economic and Environmental Feasibility of Renewable Energy Integrated Grid for Charging Three-Wheeler Electric Vehicles in Dhaka City
detail.abstract: Bangladesh's growing energy demand and urbanization necessitate a transition to renewable energy to address dependency on fossil fuels, environmental degradation, and energy shortages. This study uses HOMER (Hybrid Optimization of Multiple Energy Resources) Pro software for system design and optimization to evaluate the feasibility of hybrid solar and wind-powered charging stations for electric three-wheelers (E3Ws) in Dhaka city. By integrating photovoltaic (PV) systems and wind turbines into the charging infrastructure, the proposed strategy achieves a 62% reduction in CO2 emissions compared to grid-only alternatives while maintaining economic viability with a 1.46% increase in net present cost. The analysis considers the city's solar irradiance and wind potential, demonstrating that a hybrid approach effectively reduces reliance on grid electricity, supports financial sustainability through excess energy sales, and enhances energy resilience. This strategy aligns with global sustainability goals, promoting cleaner transportation and renewable energy use. The findings provide a scalable solution for balancing economic and environmental considerations in Dhaka's electric vehicle (EV) ecosystem and urban energy planning.

title: Economic Development and Structural Transformation: Analyzing Pakistan's Case

detail.title: Economic Development and Structural Transformation: Analyzing Pakistan's Case
detail.abstract: The experience of developed countries suggests that structural transformation of the economy is closelylinked to economic development.During the process of structural transformation, economy transitions from the production of low-value primary products to high-value, and high-tech sophisticated products, and workers move from low-productivity to highproductivity sectors. As a result, national income increases and workers also become better off due to increase in their productivity and wages. An analysis of data for the period 1970 to 2015 suggests that the contribution of agriculture to GDP has declined over the years but in terms of employer it is stillthe largest sector of the economy. The contribution of services sector has increased substantially but without commensurate increase in employment. The manufacturing sector is stagnant both in terms of its contribution to GDP and employment since 1970. This sector is thus the Achilles Heel of Pakistan's economy.Contrary to Pakistan's experience, its comparator countries like South Korea and Malaysia have reduced their reliance on traditional sectors of economy via accelerated process of structural transformation. They have moved from the 'periphery' of the product space to the 'core' during this transformation. Pakistan's production/exports are still concentrated in the periphery of the product space. Constraints hindering Pakistan from producing high-tech, high-value goods are basically twofold. First, Pakistan has specialized in sectors like textile andleather. The skill set acquired from producing these products is hardly relevant for the production of high-tech capital-intensive and consumer durables. Second, public policies such as industrial policy, technology policy, and innovation policy etc. have not been effectively utilized to facilitate the jump from the periphery to the core of the product space.Four lows i.e. low complexity of economy, low growth of manufacturing,low innovation, and low competitiveness are the real constraints for economic development in Pakistan. Accordingly, paper suggests that Pakistan needs to focus on accelerating the process of structural transformation by establishing linkages between all sectors of the economy. Measures like identification of products nearby product space, picking strategic sectors and products for industrial policy intervention, developing clusters, focusing on SMEs and RNFE for rural structural transformation, and gearing public policies towards fostering productivity, innovation and national competitiveness etc. are recommended for economic development.

title: Application of Marine Greens in Climate Change Mitigation

detail.title: Application of Marine Greens in Climate Change Mitigation
detail.abstract: Marine greens, including macroalgae (seaweeds) and seagrasses, play a significant role in regulating the global carbon cycle and offer promising nature-based solutions for climate change mitigation. These marine primary producers exhibit high rates of carbon fixation, contribute to long-term carbon sequestration through biomass accumulation and sediment burial, and support coastal blue carbon ecosystems. This study examines the applications of marine greens in climate change mitigation, focusing on their potential for carbon sequestration, greenhouse gas reduction, and ecosystem-based adaptation. Marine greens also provide co-benefits such as nutrient removal, shoreline stabilization, biodiversity enhancement, and support for sustainable livelihoods. Emerging applications, including large-scale seaweed cultivation, biochar production, and carbon offset frameworks, are discussed alongside challenges related to scalability, ecological impacts, and policy integration. The study highlights the need for improved quantification of carbon sequestration pathways, standardized accounting methods, and supportive governance structures to fully harness the climate mitigation potential of marine greens. Integrating marine greens into climate strategies can enhance mitigation efforts while delivering ecological and socioeconomic benefits in coastal and marine environments.

title: A Proposal for an Excessivist Social Welfare Ordering

detail.title: A Proposal for an Excessivist Social Welfare Ordering
detail.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a class of generalised utilitarian social welfare orderings that we call "Excessivist". The Excessivist Social Welfare Ordering (eSWO) judges incomes above a fixed threshold as detrimental for society. To accomplish this, the identification of a richness or affluence line is necessary; we employ a fixed, exogenous line of excess. We define an eSWO in the form of a weighted sum of individual's incomes. This requires introducing a vector of weights. We allow the weights to be both positive (for individuals below the line) and negative (for individuals above); moreover, they ensure that the higher the number of excessively rich individuals, the greater the negative impact the society has, and vice versa. Then we introduce ethical concerns through an axiomatic approach. We proved that the proposed ordering satisfies the following axioms: Continuity above and below the threshold (Ca,Cb), Rank Separability (RS), absolute Aversion to Excessive Richness (AER), Pigou Dalton Transfer (PDT), Ratio Scale Comparability (RSC) and Strong Pareto below the threshold (SPb), Population Replication at the threshold (PRt). We show an empirical application of how the ordering works for two distributions of consumptions in Ghana (2013, 2017).

title: The Economics of Inequality

detail.title: The Economics of Inequality
detail.abstract: (This paper analyses the changing paradigms on economic inequality and the baneful effects it can have on economic growth, development of institutions, financial, political and economic stability, and subjective wellbeing etc. After analyzing inequality purely from economic perspective, paper takes stock of inequality in Pakistan. The factors responsible for extreme inequality in Pakistan are almost structural in nature. Skewed distribution of productive assets, ineffective taxation system, rent seeking, unequal opportunities of education, and regional disparities due to urban- biased public policies have been identified as main drivers of inequality. The paper gives two sets of recommendations i.e. revolutionary (the high road) and evolutionary (the low road) for addressing the problem of economic inequality in Pakistan. The paper concludes that status quo is not a choice as frustration of the people with the system is fast increasing. Author)

detail.title: Exploring the Effects of Five Local Dimensions on Local Development in South Africa via Multivariate Granger Causality Test

detail.abstract: Granger causality analysis is a popular method for inference on directed interactions in complex systems of many variables. One shortcoming of the standard framework for Granger causality is that it only allows for examination of interactions between single univariate variables within a system, usually conditioned on other variables. However, interactions in a system do not necessarily take place between single variables but may occur among groups or "ensembles" of variables. This study employs the Granger causality test within a multivariate cointegration and errorcorrection framework to investigate the relationship between local development, infrastructure, productivity, quality of life, equity and environmental sustainability at a local level in South Africa. The study covers the annual sample from 1994 to 2014. The main findings of this study are that, in the short-run, there is unidirectional Granger causality running from local infrastructure to productivity, and from equity to quality of life in South Africa. Bidirectional Granger causality is found between quality of life and productivity. Environmental sustainability and local development also have bidirectional Granger causality. In the long-run there is unidirectional Granger causality running from five local factors: local infrastructure, local productivity, quality of life, equity and local environmental sustainability to local development. Additionally, the study was extended to examine the dynamic interaction between the variables in the system through the forecast error variance decomposition and impulse response function analyses. In line with the finding of Granger causality, all the variables behaved endogenously in the long-run. Thus, the variables Granger-causes each other in the long-run even though there might be deviations in the short-run.

title: Large Language Model-Driven Analysis of Supply Risk Dynamics in Global Electric Vehicle Supply Chain
affiliations: Tsinghua University, University of Groningen, Tsinghua University, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Institute of Urban Environment, Nanjing Forestry University and Tsinghua University - School of Environment

detail.title: Large Language Model-Driven Analysis of Supply Risk Dynamics in Global Electric Vehicle Supply Chain
detail.abstract: Driven by ambitious climate targets, the rapid growth of electric vehicles (EV) is creating complex global supply chains that are increasingly exposed to disruptions. While supply risks, such as political instability and resource scarcity, are widely recognized, systematic assessments of disruption events across the entire EV supply chain remain limited. This study employs a Large language model (LLM) with prompt engineering to identify disruption events from unstructured textual data and further analyze risk dynamics. Applying this approach to 3125 news articles from 2006 to 2025, we extract 2843 documented events and further categorize them into 50 disruption event types and 8 supply risk types, spanning 49 supply chain stages and 78 countries and regions. We find that geopolitical risks have emerged as the dominant concern in recent years. Vehicle assembly, battery manufacturing, and lithium ore extraction emerged as the most vulnerable stages. Geographic heterogeneity in risk distribution reveals the distinct roles countries play in the global EV supply chain. This proposed LLM-based framework provides actionable insights for enhancing supply chain resilience during the accelerating EV transition.

title: Emotions as Discrete Tokens for Credit Assignment

detail.title: Emotions as Discrete Tokens for Credit Assignment
detail.abstract: Current artificial intelligence systems demonstrate proficiency in short-horizon tasks through next-token prediction and dense reward signals, yet exhibit substantial limitations in long-term reasoning and planning. This paper proposes that emotions evolved as a discrete tokenization mechanism solving the credit assignment problem in continuous action spaces. We formalize this hypothesis within a reinforcement learning framework, demonstrating how discrete emotional states enable Monte Carlo Tree Search-like planning over extended time horizons by circumventing the combinatorial explosion inherent in continuous action spaces. We present mathematical analysis of why discretization at the policy level is computationally necessary, supported by evidence from neuroscience and comparative biology. Our framework suggests that autonomous agents operating in continuous environments with sparse rewards may require analogous discrete tokenization mechanisms for effective long-term planning.

title: The Effects of Internal and External Factors on Financial Risk Exposure (Stock Price Volatility) of Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. from 2015 to 2024

detail.title: The Effects of Internal and External Factors on Financial Risk Exposure (Stock Price Volatility) of Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. from 2015 to 2024

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on secondary data and does not involve human participants; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper analyses the impact of internal and external factors on the financial risk exposure of Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. during the period of 2015 to 2024 using stock price volatility as an indicator of the financial risk. The firm is very susceptible to macroeconomic condition changes, raw material prices, and financial structure because it is a significant steel manufacturer in the United States. In 2018, the additional adoption of the Trump era steel tariffs added to market uncertainty and risk exposure within the industry. Based on annual data, this paper examines the effects of firm-specific variables, leverage, liquidity, profitability, cash flow strength, and operational efficiency, and external variables, which include GDP growth, interest rate, inflation rate, exchange rate, consumer confidence, and liquidity movements of commodity prices, on the annualised stock price volatility of the company. As expected, the findings shall shed some light on the origin of financial risk in the steel industry and the significance of effective financial risk management in cyclical and policy-sensitive settings.

title: Climate Shocks, Trade Credit, and Firm Resilience in Chile

detail.title: Climate Shocks, Trade Credit, and Firm Resilience in Chile
detail.abstract: This paper studies how climate disasters propagate through production networks and how firms’ pre-existing trade credit positions shape their ability to withstand these shocks. Using the universe of electronic invoices, tax filings, and wildfire alerts in Chile from 2015 to 2024, I construct monthly buyer–supplier links and measure three exposure margins: direct hits to the focal firm, shocks to suppliers, and shocks to customers. I estimate dynamic effects using a Local-Projections DiD design accounting for timing and staggered adoption. Wildfires generate a decline in sales, purchases, and employment, and they weaken supply-chain stability by increasing partner turnover and firm exit. Pre-shock trade credit received mitigates these effects across all exposure margins. In contrast, firms that entered with large receivables face tighter liquidity and amplified losses, although they preserve more relationships, reflecting trade credit’s role as both liquidity insurance and relational capital. These results show that short-term interfirm financing arrangements shape the propagation of shocks along the production network and their resilience.

title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Contributing Factors in Bus Crashes: Integrating Passenger Injury Severity and Vehicle Damage Severity using the Frank Copula Model
affiliations: Central South University, Central South University, Monash University - Monash University Malaysia, Central South University and Central South University

detail.title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Contributing Factors in Bus Crashes: Integrating Passenger Injury Severity and Vehicle Damage Severity using the Frank Copula Model
detail.abstract: Bus crashes remain a significant public safety concern due to their potential to cause both passenger injuries and substantial vehicle damage. These two severity outcomes are interrelated, as the physical forces in high-impact crashes contribute simultaneously to occupant harm and structural damage. However, most existing studies model these outcomes independently, overlooking their statistical dependence and shared risk factors. To address this gap, this study employs a copula-based modeling framework to jointly analyze passenger injury and vehicle damage severity using bus crash data from Maryland (2015–2022). The joint estimation results reveal distinct sets of significant predictors for passenger injury severity and vehicle damage severity. For injury outcomes, the most influential variables include driver fault, airbag deployment, and safety equipment usage, underscoring the critical role of both human error and protective systems in shaping injury levels. In contrast, vehicle damage severity is more strongly associated with vehicle type, movement status at the time of impact, and mechanical condition. The inclusion of the vehicle type variable shows that school buses, despite being structurally safer, are frequently involved in crashes due to high exposure, contributing to notable damage risks. Additionally, adverse vehicle conditions and airbag deployment exhibit a strong association with disabling or destroyed damage, highlighting the role of structural integrity and energy dissipation mechanisms in post-impact outcomes. These patterns, revealed through the Copula-MNL model, reflect not only the distinct causal pathways for the two severity measures but also their shared dependence on critical safety-related factors.

title: Keep them out of It! How information externalities affect the willingness to sell personal data online
affiliations: University of Marburg, King’s College London - King's Business School and Erasmus University Rotterdam School of Law, Rotterdam Institute of Law and Economics

detail.title: Keep them out of It! How information externalities affect the willingness to sell personal data online
detail.abstract: When individuals provide their personal data online, they often disregard that this allows learning about others, too. Our large-scale online experiment reveals that individuals are less willing to provide personal data when sharing can compromise others' privacy, entailing personalized price discrimination. Compared to a benchmark without data compromise, individuals' willingness to sell data decreases when others' data is compromised with 50% or 100% probability. By applying two well-studied interventions-peer effects and a social norm focus-we explore ways to mitigate excessive data sharing, laying the ground for policy design. While peer effects, on average, increase individuals' willingness to provide personal data, making people reflect on the appropriate behavior appears to be a promising social nudge to reduce negative externalities.

title: Pakistan: Growth Diagnostics

detail.title: Pakistan: Growth Diagnostics
detail.abstract: (This paper analyses the binding constraints to sustainable economic growth in Pakistan within the growth diagnostics framework developed by Hausmann et al. Factors like limited access to finance, low returns to economic activity, and low appropriability of returns are discussed at length in the light of data and literature. Low financial inclusion, weak financial intermediation, and low human capital formation are serious concerns but do not constitute binding constraints to sustainable economic growth. Similarly, shortage of electricity, poor law and order, and security concerns are constraints to economic growth but all these problems are connected to poor institutional quality and bad governance. The critical constraints in case of Pakistan are what the growth diagnostics framework calls 'micro-risks' like weak property rights and corruption etc. The paper concludes that weak institutions and poor governance are in fact the binding constraints to economic growth. Pakistan needs to revamp its slow-moving judicial system to enforce property rights and contracts. Pakistan should introduce structural reforms to improve functioning of institutions and governance. Private and public sectors need to join hands to foster productivity. Such reforms are not only doable but desirable to ignite growth, when the country is faced with scarcity of capital and resources. Author)

title: Discrimination against Women Representation in the Nigerian Judiciary

detail.title: Discrimination against Women Representation in the Nigerian Judiciary
detail.abstract: This paper examines the continued underrepresentation of women in the Nigerian judiciary despite the increasing percentage of female participation in the legal profession. It identifies key barriers limiting women's advancement in the legal profession, such as procedural requirements for promotion, cultural and patriarchal norms, and the lack of mentorship and structured support. Through a comparison of historical developments, current statistics, and societal influences, the study highlights how deeply entrenched structural and cultural factors continue to restrict women's representation in senior judicial positions. The paper further highlights the existing efforts by organisations such as the International Association of Women Judges (IAWJ), the International Federation of Women Lawyers (FIDA Nigeria), and the Women Advocates Research and Documentation Center (WARDC), geared towards women's advancement. Finally, it proposes recommendations to improve women's participation, such as constitutional and statutory reforms, the introduction of gender quotas in judicial appointments, and the establishment of formal mentorship programs. Addressing these barriers is very important because women's participation promotes legitimacy, public trust, access to justice, and broader societal impact within Nigeria's legal system.

title: Estimating income inequality in rural Roman Egypt

detail.title: Estimating income inequality in rural Roman Egypt
detail.abstract: This study examines income inequality in rural Roman Egypt in 1st century AD on the basis of data from papyri for the village of Tebtunis. It identifies and collects data from papyrological sources for three social classes - workers, priests, and village elites – to assemble a social table for the population of Tebtunis. The evidence suggests that inequality and the degree of extraction of incomes by elites was not excessively high, reflecting the rural setting and limited heterogeneity in incomes at the top compared to urban settings and the Roman empire as a whole. A driver of inequality is found to be the highly regressive poll tax, which this study argues increases both the Gini coefficient and inequality extraction ratio, adding further evidence for the role of regressive taxation in increasing inequality in pre-industrial societies.

title: Does Real-Time Monitoring Expand State Capacity? Evidence from Environmental Enforcement

detail.title: Does Real-Time Monitoring Expand State Capacity? Evidence from Environmental Enforcement
detail.abstract: Real-time monitoring technologies are increasingly used to strengthen regulatory enforcement, yet it remains unclear whether they expand state capacity or primarily reshape the allocation of scarce enforcement resources. This paper studies satellite-based deforestation alerts in the Brazilian Amazon, combining annual forest loss data, near-real-time alerts, and georeferenced enforcement actions from 2010–2020. Exploiting variation in the timing of alerts at a granular geographic level, I estimate the effect of monitoring alerts on enforcement behavior. Alerts generate a statistically significant short-run increase in formal enforcement actions, but much of this effect reflects a reallocation of inspections forward in time rather than large increases in aggregate enforcement activity. I estimate that approximately 4.5 percent of enforcement actions can be attributed to monitoring alerts. Effects are concentrated in areas where violations are difficult to predict absent real-time monitoring, indicating that monitoring primarily improves targeting rather than substantially expanding enforcement intensity.

title: Time-Dependent Affordability Risk in Consumer Auto Finance: Implications for Household Credit Risk and Macroeconomic Stress Transmission

detail.title: Time-Dependent Affordability Risk in Consumer Auto Finance: Implications for Household Credit Risk and Macroeconomic Stress Transmission
