detail.abstract: Traditional affordability metrics in consumer auto lending rely on static, point-in-time assessments that may fail to capture default risk when income is volatile, and payment obligations change over time. This paper introduces time-dependent affordability measures that incorporate income volatility and payment structure dynamics. Using a sample of 47,328 auto loans that originated between 2022 and 2024, we show that borrowers with volatile income streams default at rates two to three times higher than otherwise similar borrowers with stable income, even when traditional affordability metrics appear comparable. Loans with deferred payment increases exhibit concentrated defaults around payment shock periods. We develop a risk classification framework combining these dimensions and document a 12–18 percent improvement in out-of-sample default prediction. A stylized dynamic model rationalizes these patterns and highlights the role of strategic default. The findings have implications for household credit risk assessment, macroeconomic stress testing, and the design of sustainable lending contracts.

title: The Algorithm of Universe: A Divergence-Integration Principle for Complex Systems

detail.title: The Algorithm of Universe: A Divergence-Integration Principle for Complex Systems
detail.abstract: I propose a general dynamical principle-the "Algorithm of Universe" (AoU)governing complex systems: Divergence from a seed state, Saturation against capacity limits, and Convergence toward integration or collapse. I formalize this as a coupled ODE system and provide rigorous empirical validation in one domain: knowledge evolution, where the model achieves r = 0.97 correlation with 75 years of scientometric data and successfully predicts held-out trajectories. I then demonstrate qualitative consistency across additional domains: computing (mainframes → PCs → cloud/AI), demographics (population decline in technologically advanced nations), and labor (automation consolidating human work). Finally, I propose testable mappings to physics (stellar evolution as divergence-convergence cycles) and biology (speciation and ecological integration). This paper establishes AoU as a cross-disciplinary framework; domain-specific validation is invited.

title: A Curvature-Based Perspective on Regulatory Dynamics in Conscious Experience

detail.title: A Curvature-Based Perspective on Regulatory Dynamics in Conscious Experience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Regulatory practices such as somatic awareness, trauma-focused interventions, flow states, and rhythmic breathing consistently produce non-linear transitions in conscious experience that are poorly captured by linear or content-based models. While these approaches differ in technique, they often exhibit structurally similar regulatory effects. This paper introduces a curvature-based perspective on conscious experience, treating it as a dynamic state space in which rigidity, flexibility, and transition correspond to geometric properties rather than representational content. Within this framework, regulatory change is interpreted as the redistribution of local curvature rather than the elimination or modification of mental states. Time is reinterpreted at the experiential level as a measure of state deformation, independent of physical temporal metrics. This reinterpretation does not deny or replace physical time; rather, it decouples experiential change from clock-based duration, allowing equal physical intervals to correspond to unequal experiential deformation lengths depending on system rigidity and curvature. The proposed framework, referred to as the Consciousness Curvature Framework (CCFy), does not constitute a clinical, neuroscientific, or physical theory. Instead, it offers a conceptual coordinate system for organizing diverse regulatory phenomena and generating falsifiable qualitative predictions through minimal simulations. By reframing regulation in geometric terms, the framework clarifies why structurally distinct interventions often yield similar experiential outcomes.

title: Parameter Knowledge Justification Index (PKJI): A Feature-Level Decision Metric for Value-Cost Governance in Product Development

detail.title: Parameter Knowledge Justification Index (PKJI): A Feature-Level Decision Metric for Value-Cost Governance in Product Development
detail.abstract: Feature-level decision-making in product development often suffers from ambiguity when balancing customer expectations with economic feasibility. Traditional tools such as Quality Function Deployment (QFD) [2] effectively translate the voice of the customer into technical parameters but do not provide a mechanism for cost-value justification. This paper introduces the Parameter Knowledge Justification Index (PKJI) as a quantitative decision metric that integrates Customer Value (CV) [1] and Lifecycle Cost (LCC) to enable transparent and data-driven governance. PKJI operates in two modes: Target PKJI, based on planned cost and expected value, and Observed PKJI, based on actual cost and realized value. The proposed framework defines CV as the weighted sum of economic contributions and customer concern weights, while lifecycle cost is segmented into four blocks [6]-design, development, industrialization, and operation-using proportional weights. Decision thresholds are established to classify features into Go, Conditional Approval, or Reject, ensuring alignment with portfolio-level value-to-cost benchmarks. A worked example demonstrates the application of PKJI for feature evaluation, highlighting its potential to improve cost discipline, accelerate early kill decisions, and enhance portfolio alignment. Future work will explore integration with QFD for holistic governance.

title: GHDP™ I — Time as a Binding Economic Constraint

detail.title: GHDP™ I — Time as a Binding Economic Constraint

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces GHDP™ (Gross Human Dynamics Product) as a macro-financial framework that treats time as a binding economic constraint rather than an exogenous background variable.

The paper formalizes human temporal capacity as a systemic limit and examines how acceleration beyond this limit produces divergence between system performance and human adaptive bandwidth. GHDP™ is defined as an analytical framework, not as a wellbeing index, outcome score, or post-hoc adjustment to GDP.

This paper serves as the definitional foundation of the GHDP™ series.

title: Water, Risk, and Human Behavior: Integrating Evidence From Economics, Hydrology, and Environmental Policy

detail.title: Water, Risk, and Human Behavior: Integrating Evidence From Economics, Hydrology, and Environmental Policy

keywords: and Human Behavior: Integrating Evidence From Economics

detail.abstract: Water systems across the world face intensifying pressures from population growth, climate change, institutional rigidity, and shifting social preferences. Understanding how individuals, firms, and governments adapt to scarcity and hydrologic uncertainty requires an interdisciplinary perspective integrating economics, behavioral science, engineering, and ecology. This paper synthesizes insights from empirical and theoretical contributions in water economics, environmental management, and resource policy— drawing heavily on studies examining residential water demand, agricultural adaptation, ecosystem-service valuation, water-rights institutions, and risk mitigation. Several themes emerge: (1) human behavior plays a central role in shaping water outcomes; (2) institutions mediate hydrologic constraints; (3) uncertainty about tipping points accelerates resource degradation; and (4) integrated management approaches offer pathways toward resilience when aligned with governance structures and behavioral motivations. The paper concludes by identifying cross-sectoral lessons for improving water governance.

title:
GHDP™ II — What GHDP™ is Not 
Boundary Conditions, Invalid Extensions, and Citation Discipline

detail.title:
GHDP™ II — What GHDP™ is Not 
Boundary Conditions, Invalid Extensions, and Citation Discipline

detail.abstract:
As the term “GHDP” has appeared across academic, policy, and applied contexts, its
meaning has diverged substantially. This paper establishes the negative definition of
GHDP™ (Gross Human Dynamics Product) by specifying what GHDP™ is not, the
boundary conditions under which it cannot be validly applied, and the citation
discipline required to prevent conceptual drift.
GHDP™ is neither a wellbeing index, a human development metric, nor a GDP-adjusted
outcome score. It does not measure welfare, happiness, inclusion, or progress.
Instead, GHDP™ is a macro-financial framework that models human temporal
capacity as a binding systemic constraint under acceleration.
This paper formalizes exclusion criteria, identifies invalid extensions, and sets citation
standards to ensure terminological integrity across economic, policy, and
computational research.

title: Management Challenges Regarding Information Management in Public Organization Structures

detail.title: Management Challenges Regarding Information Management in Public Organization Structures
detail.abstract: The activity of public sector managers is constantly subject to challenges arising from legislative changes, ad-litteram compliance with legislation, but also from demands from citizens. The article aims to analyze the degree of compliance of county council organizations , prefectural institutions, city and town halls in the NorthEast Region of Romania with regard to the degree of publication of information of public interest. The analysis was carried out by processing data from 2024, monitored by the General Secretariat of the Government and displayed on the website www.sgg.ro. Secondary data analysis was used to highlight the situation of ex officio publication of information of public interest. The study highlighted the fact that public institutions with a more complex organizational structure, with a larger number of employees, which have specialized IT departments, record higher percentages of compliance with regard to the publication of information of public interest, while small city halls with a small number of employees hardly reach the 50% compliance percentage. The institution of the prefect record the highest average compliance among the institutions analyzed.

title: The Gatekeeper Effect: Relational Sovereignty and the "Catalytic Hub" of Leadership in Thai Secondary Education

detail.title: The Gatekeeper Effect: Relational Sovereignty and the "Catalytic Hub" of Leadership in Thai Secondary Education

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted in strict adherence to the ethical guidelines for human subjects research. The research protocol, including all survey instruments and interview guides, was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee in Human Research, National Institute of Development Administration (ECNIDA) (Protocol ID2025/0084)

detail.abstract:
This study challenges the prevailing horizontal conceptualization of social
capital by documenting a vertically concentrated form of relational power within elite
Thai secondary schools. While Western administrative models emphasize distributed
leadership and polycentric governance, this research uncovers a tightly centralized
architecture of institutional permeability. Using an explanatory mixed-methods
design—integrating forensic access logs (𝑁 = 36) and 66 in-depth interviews—
we investigate the structural mechanisms that govern school-environment interactions.
Findings reveal a decisive Gatekeeper Effect: formal bureaucratic protocols for school
access achieved a success rate of only 13.6%, whereas informal, Director-mediated
referrals achieved a 100% success rate. This empirical disparity demonstrates that
de jure state authority has been functionally displaced by the de facto, trust-based
networks of school leadership. We theorize the School Director as a "Catalytic Hub,"
the indispensable relational node who converts symbolic capital (Baramee) into
kinetic network activation. This hub-and-spoke topology facilitates exceptional
operational agility but induces a paradox of "Fragile Efficiency"—a system optimized
for high performance yet acutely vulnerable to "Succession Shocks." This article contributes to social capital theory by proposing a model of Concentrated Relationality
and advances leadership theory by deconstructing the "Catalytic Hub" as a prerequisite
for service delivery in fragile state contexts

title: Digital Security as a Human Problem, not a Technical One

detail.title: Digital Security as a Human Problem, not a Technical One

detail.abstract: Contemporary discussions of cybersecurity failures often frame breaches as the result of technical shortcomings or individual user mistakes. This paper argues that such explanations are incomplete and systematically misleading. Most successful attacks do not exploit failures in cryptography or infrastructure, but predictable features of human cognition operating under conditions of uncertainty, time pressure, and organizational constraint. Drawing on insights from behavioral psychology, cognitive science, and security architecture, this paper reframes cybersecurity as a sociotechnical problem in which human behavior is not an anomaly but a core component of the attack surface. It examines how social engineering exploits universal cognitive patterns, why the concept of “user error” obscures underlying design failures, and how traditional threat modeling neglects the realities of human decision-making. The paper further explores human-in-the-loop security and Zero Trust architecture as approaches that implicitly acknowledge human limitations by reshaping incentives and decision processes rather than relying on idealized user behavior. Ultimately, it argues that robust security systems are those designed around how humans actually think and act, making secure behavior the default rather than the exception.

title: Culturally Effective Organization: Revisiting the Role of Employers in Workforce Development in Kathmandu Valley

detail.title: Culturally Effective Organization: Revisiting the Role of Employers in Workforce Development in Kathmandu Valley
detail.abstract: This study examines the culturally effective organization: revisiting the role of employers in workforce development in Kathmandu Valley. Workforce development is the dependable variables. The independent variables are job security, organization culture, training and development, cross-cultural competence, recognition and rewards, and leadership styles. The study is based on primary data with 165 respondents. To achieve the purpose of the study, structured questionnaire is prepared. The correlation coefficients and regression models are estimated to test the significance and the culturally effective organization and workforce development in Kathmandu Valley.

title: From Requistion to Payment: Mapping and Mitigating Internal Fraud Vulnerabilities within Digital Procurement-to-Pay Systems for Public Works

detail.abstract: The rapid digitization of public works procurement has introduced significant efficiencies but has simultaneously exposed infrastructure projects to sophisticated internal fraud vulnerabilities. This study investigates the mapping and mitigation of fraudulent activities within digital Procurementto-Pay (P2P) systems in the United States public sector. Anchored in the Fraud Triangle Theory and Agency Theory, the research utilizes a mixed-methods approach-comprising a systematic literature review, a descriptive survey, and semi-structured interviews-to identify systemic weaknesses through the end of the 2022 fiscal year. Findings indicate that inadequate access controls (75%) and a lack of segregation of duties (65%) are the primary catalysts for internal malfeasance. The study reveals that while digital transformation aims to enhance transparency, it often creates "information silos" that facilitate data manipulation and internal-external collusion. This paper proposes a comprehensive Mitigation Framework centered on Defense-in-Depth strategies, including the automation of role-based access controls and the implementation of continuous data analytics. By aligning technological safeguards with the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR, 2022), this research provides public works agencies with a scalable roadmap to protect taxpayer investments from the multi-billion dollar threat of occupational fraud. title: The Supply Chain Oracle: A Predictive Model for Detecting Cost Inflation and Bid Rigging in Large-Scale Infrastructure Contracts Using Commodity Indices and Forensic Price Benchmarking

detail.title: The Supply Chain Oracle: A Predictive Model for Detecting Cost Inflation and Bid Rigging in Large-Scale Infrastructure Contracts Using Commodity Indices and Forensic Price Benchmarking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflicting interest
declarations.funderStatement: no funding received

detail.abstract: The procurement of large-scale infrastructure is critically vulnerable to two intertwined threats: genuine cost inflation from volatile commodity markets and artificial price manipulation through sophisticated bid-rigging cartels. Traditional detection methods, being reactive and analog, struggle to distinguish between these phenomena, leading to significant financial losses and eroded public trust. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating "The Supply Chain Oracle," a predictive model that integrates real-time commodity price indices with forensic price benchmarking to proactively detect collusive bidding. The research employs a quantitative, positivist methodology, constructing a multivariate econometric model to establish a dynamic, commodity-justified benchmark price for infrastructure projects. Statistically significant anomalies positive deviations of actual bid prices from this benchmark are identified and rigorously tested against a verified dataset of corrupt and non-corrupt contracts. The model demonstrates strong diagnostic accuracy, with 74.3% sensitivity, 85.7% specificity, and an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.87. Furthermore, these anomaly scores are calibrated into a probabilistic risk index, providing a practical tool for audit prioritization. The findings reveal that sectors like railways and bridges exhibit disproportionately high anomaly rates, aligning with theories of cartel stability in oligopolistic markets. This research concludes that commodity-justified price benchmarking offers a transformative, evidence-based approach for procurement oversight, shifting the paradigm from reactive investigation to proactive, intelligence-driven prevention and safeguarding of public funds.

title: Operationalizing Curiosity: Structural Repair of Coordination Failures in High-Stakes Systems

detail.title: Operationalizing Curiosity: Structural Repair of Coordination Failures in High-Stakes Systems
detail.abstract: Persistent human conflict is commonly attributed to misinformation, bias, or moral failure. These explanations fail to account for coordination breakdowns among informed, well-intentioned agents operating under shared goals. This paper proposes an alternative account: that much human conflict arises from common-knowledge failure under conditions of temporal and informational uncertainty. When agents lack signals that are both observable and known to be observable by others, coordination becomes structurally underdetermined. Within this framework, curiosity is reclassified not as a personality trait or virtue, but as a system state that emerges when defensive gating is reduced by the presence of a robust public coordination device. We introduce a minimal operational model for diagnosing coordination breakdowns, propose a latency-based metric for trust formation, and demonstrate how explicit governing artifacts function as low-cost structural repairs.

title: Deep Learning Applications for Fault Detection and Protection in Smart Grids

detail.title: Deep Learning Applications for Fault Detection and Protection in Smart Grids
detail.abstract: The rapid evolution of smart grids has introduced unprecedented levels of complexity in power system operation, monitoring, and protection. Traditional fault detection and protection mechanisms, largely based on predefined thresholds and rule-based logic, are increasingly inadequate in addressing the dynamic, data-intensive, and decentralized nature of modern power networks. This study critically examines the application of deep learning techniques for fault detection and protection in smart grids, with particular emphasis on convolutional neural networks, deep reinforcement learning, and hybrid artificial intelligence frameworks. Through a structured synthesis of recent peer-reviewed literature, this research evaluates the effectiveness, adaptability, and limitations of deep learning-based fault management systems. The findings reveal that deep learning models significantly enhance fault classification accuracy, resilience to noise, and adaptability under varying grid conditions. However, challenges remain in terms of data dependency, real-time deployment, interpretability, and integration with existing protection infrastructure. The study concludes that while deep learning represents a transformative advancement for smart grid protection, its practical adoption requires standardized evaluation frameworks, hybrid system architectures, and closer alignment with operational constraints. Future research directions and implementation strategies are proposed to bridge the gap between theoretical performance and real-world deployment.

title: How Power Distance Belief Affects Consumer Satisfaction After Data Breach
affiliations: , University of Texas at San Antonio, University of Texas at San Antonio and Rice University

detail.title: How Power Distance Belief Affects Consumer Satisfaction After Data Breach
detail.abstract: This article investigates how Power Distance Belief (PDB) influences consumer satisfaction after a data breach announcement. Seven studies employing diverse methodologies-including both primary and secondary data-across multiple industry contexts and participant samples, show high-PDB individuals exhibit greater satisfaction with the company affected by a data breach even after the data breach announcement. This effect is driven by high-PDB individuals' tendency to place greater trust in the ability and benevolence of higher-order entities, which increases their confidence in the company's breach response. Further, the impact of PDB is more strongly driven by ability-based trust than by benevolence-based trust. Finally, when comparing different types of remedies, consumer-led remedies improve satisfaction for both high-and low-PDB individuals, whereas company-led remedies are less effective among low-PDB individuals. Overall, this research provides theoretical and practical insights into how individual differences shape consumer responses to corporate crises like a data breach.

title: Technologies of the Self in Michel Foucault's Late Philosophy: Ancient Roots and Contemporary Interpretations

detail.title: Technologies of the Self in Michel Foucault's Late Philosophy: Ancient Roots and Contemporary Interpretations
detail.abstract: This study elucidates Michel Foucault's concept of-technologies of the self‖ as developed in his late works, with particular emphasis on its ancient Greek and Roman antecedents. It examines how these practices historically served as modes of ethical selfformation and how they challenge contemporary forms of subjectivation under neoliberal governance. Drawing on Foucault's analyses in The History of Sexuality, Volume III (The Care of the Self) and his Collège de France lectures, the article traces the genealogy of self-practices (askēsis, epimeleia heautou) as both philosophical exercises and political acts. The originality of the study lies in its systematic juxtaposition of Foucault's genealogical approach with Slavoj Žižek's Lacanian-Marxist critique of ideology, desire, and symbolic constraints. Integrating recent scholarship, the article demonstrates the continuing relevance-and the dangers-of such practices in neoliberal societies. It concludes that ancient techniques of the self foreground the possibility of ethical autonomy beyond external normativity while simultaneously revealing the persistent risk of their capture by unconscious libidinal investments and capitalist imperatives.

title: From Patronage to Performance: How Rent Management Shaped Thailand and Malaysia's Auto Futures

detail.title: From Patronage to Performance: How Rent Management Shaped Thailand and Malaysia's Auto Futures
detail.abstract: This paper examines how political settlements shaped industrial upgrading in the automotive sectors of Thailand and Malaysia through the allocation and management of rents. Despite similar ambitions, Malaysia's dominant-party regime pursued a protected, politically driven national car strategy, resulting in limited competitiveness, while Thailand's fragmented competitive-clientelist system adopted disciplined, performance-based rents that fostered global export success. By dynamically tracing rent evolution across multiple decades, the analysis reveals critical path dependencies: Malaysia's initial weak enforcement entrenched patronage interests, restricting later adaptability, whereas Thailand's early performance pressures institutionalized capabilitybuilding. The findings contribute to political economy literature by emphasizing that rent effectiveness is determined less by regime type and more by institutionalized enforcement mechanisms and strategic alignment with global market conditions. These findings carry implications for contemporary industrial policy debates in late-industrializing economies facing global competition and technological transition.

title: Intelligent Protection and Control of Renewable Energy Systems using CNN-based Fault Analysis

detail.title: Intelligent Protection and Control of Renewable Energy Systems using CNN-based Fault Analysis
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of renewable energy systems (RES) has created both opportunities and challenges in energy management, particularly in ensuring reliability and fault resilience. Traditional fault detection systems, often relay-based, are insufficient for handling complex, dynamic conditions in modern hybrid energy systems. This study investigates the application of convolutional neural networks (CNN) for intelligent fault detection, classification, and protection in RES, including wind farms, photovoltaic (PV) systems, and microgrids. A CNN-based model was developed and trained on real-time operational data, capturing a variety of fault scenarios such as short-circuit, overvoltage, and line-to-ground faults. The results demonstrate that the CNN approach significantly outperforms conventional relay-based systems and other AI models, achieving higher accuracy, faster detection times, and more reliable classification of multi-source faults. The study highlights the potential of CNN-based fault analysis in enhancing grid stability, improving predictive maintenance, and enabling adaptive protection strategies in renewable energy operations. The findings suggest that integrating intelligent fault detection systems into RES can substantially improve operational reliability and pave the way for more sustainable and resilient energy networks.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Fault Diagnosis Techniques in Modern Power Systems

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Fault Diagnosis Techniques in Modern Power Systems
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have emerged as critical tools for fault diagnosis in modern power systems. This study examines the implementation and comparative performance of AI-based fault detection and classification (FDC) models, focusing on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), temporal convolutional networks (TCNs), deep reinforcement learning (DRL), and hybrid AI methods. We explore their effectiveness in addressing challenges inherent to traditional fault diagnosis, including delayed response times, limited adaptability, and low classification accuracy. The study finds that hybrid AI approaches, particularly those combining CNN and gated recurrent unit (GRU) architectures, demonstrate superior accuracy and adaptability in real-time fault detection. Furthermore, temporal and DRL models show promise in predictive fault localization under dynamic system conditions. Despite these advances, challenges such as computational cost, data sparsity, and model interpretability remain. Overall, AI integration enhances the operational reliability of power systems, supporting smart grid development and predictive maintenance frameworks. The study provides a comprehensive synthesis of current methodologies, highlights key performance trends, and outlines directions for future research.

title: The Crisis, Struggle and Ethical Reconstruction of Sovereignty in Bangladesh: Insaf Orientation and Cognitive Sovereignty in the Thought of Sharif Osman Hadi

No human participants, patients, case studies, or empirical data collection was involved. detail.abstract:
The 2024 July–August mass mobilization in Bangladesh toppled an entrenched regime, challenging conventional sovereignty narratives centred on territorial security and economic dependency. This study respecifies the conventional understanding of sovereignty by integrating moral legitimacy (Insaf) and epistemic autonomy (Cognitive Autonomy, CA) as constitutive, rather than peripheral, elements. Drawing on Sharif Osman Hadi’s (1993–2025) political thought, it intervenes through his concepts of “Insaf Orientation”—a justice-centred normative architecture—and “Cognitive Sovereignty,” which prioritises epistemic insulation from external hegemony. Phase I (Jan 2026) will employ a qualitative interpretive methodology to conduct thematic analysis.
The central claim posits the Hadi Framework formalized as S = T + M + CA + I—a composite rather than arithmetical formulation, here military capacity (M) is normatively constrained by moral legitimacy
It advances an alternative ethical–political model for South Asia’s fragile states, transcending the ‘dependent state’ paradigm by foregrounding justice-centred legitimacy and epistemic autonomy.
This paper is presented as a conceptual and interpretive framework rather than a finalized empirical model; its primary contribution lies in retheorizing sovereignty through the normative lenses of justice (Insaf) and cognitive autonomy, grounded in the post–July 2024 political conjuncture of Bangladesh.
Ultimately, this study re-specifies the parameters of South Asian statecraft, offering a dignity-based model for fragile states.

detail.abstract: We investigate the behavior of an adaptive algorithmic trading system under conditions of regime compression, defined as persistent reduction in regime diversity and transition entropy. Using a strictly observational protocol-fixed market data, fixed system logic, and no parameter intervention-we repeatedly evaluate system perception, decision gating, execution, and portfolio outcomes. Empirical results show rapid regime convergence, suppressed adaptive autonomy, and stable execution behavior despite deteriorating profitability. Losses remain bounded and non-chaotic, suggesting that adaptive restraint is an endogenous and coherent response rather than system failure. This study contributes to the literature on regime-switching and adaptive trading by introducing a physiological framing of system behavior, highlighting the rationality of suppressed learning under informational scarcity. Implications extend to risk management, model evaluation, and the design of adaptive mechanisms capable of detecting and responding to decompression events.

title: From Pebbles to Pixels: A Global History of Games and Play

detail.title: From Pebbles to Pixels: A Global History of Games and Play
detail.abstract: This paper contends that the history of games is not merely a collection of cultural curiosities but a continuous narrative of how human societies externalise cognition, values, and power through structured systems of play. From the tactile manipulation of bones and stones to the algorithmic infrastructures of persistent digital worlds, games demonstrate how people model conflict, cooperation, scarcity, and possibility. Tracing this evolution across seven distinct phases, the paper explores how games have transformed. These phases include handmade games as proto-administrative tools, the codification of rules as transmissible knowledge, industrial standardisation and mass leisure, mechanisation and machine opponents, the rise of networked persistence, the infrastructural turn in digital play, game economics and psychological impacts and community. By situating games within this framework, the paper positions them as architectural structures that both reflect and produce modes of organisation. Rather than viewing games as mere outcomes of technological progress, this study proposes that they are formative technologies in their own right. These mechanisms train cognition, distribute power, and structure attention. Understanding games through this lens illuminates how the act of play has evolved into a pivotal instrument of 21st-century social and technological life.

title: Deep Learning-based Fault Detection and Protection Strategies for Wind Farm Power Systems

detail.title: Deep Learning-based Fault Detection and Protection Strategies for Wind Farm Power Systems
detail.abstract: Wind farm power systems have become increasingly complex due to high penetration levels, variable operating conditions, and stringent grid-code requirements. These complexities have exposed limitations in conventional fault detection and protection mechanisms, particularly under non-linear and non-stationary conditions. This study examines deep learning-based fault detection and protection strategies applied to wind farm power systems, focusing on convolutional neural networks, hybrid deep learning architectures, and physics-informed models. A comprehensive synthesis of recent experimental and analytical studies is conducted to evaluate performance, reliability, and deployment feasibility. The findings indicate that deep learning approaches significantly enhance fault classification accuracy, reduce response time, and improve adaptability compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, integrating deep learning with numerical relays, IoT platforms, and predictive maintenance frameworks strengthens system resilience and operational efficiency. The study concludes that deep learning-driven protection strategies represent a transformative pathway for next-generation wind farm power systems, while also highlighting limitations related to data dependency, explainability, and real-time implementation.

title: A Nearby Wake-Up Call for Price Reaction Dynamics
affiliations: Banque de France - Economic Study and Research Division, Universidad de Chile and Universidad Adolfo Ibanez

detail.title: A Nearby Wake-Up Call for Price Reaction Dynamics
detail.abstract: We propose and empirically test a new explanation for competitive price reactions of consumable goods: the nearby wake-up call. An item’s price change in one store prompts local competitors to reassess its intrinsic value by learning about market conditions, thereby increasing price homogeneity across stores. However, nearby competitors are more attentive, leading to further price homogeneity among them. We structure our empirical analysis around a stylized learning model that links competitors’ attention to their geographical distance from the first-moving store. Using daily price data and stores’ geolocation, our results support the nearby wake-up call explanation through multiple validity analyses.

title: Why Existing Global Trade Corridors Fail under Polycrisis Conditions

detail.abstract: This paper examines why existing global trade corridors increasingly fail under conditions of polycrisis, despite decades of capacity expansion and operational optimization. Using a historical-comparative systems analysis of major trade disruptions between 1990 and 2025, the study identifies recurring structural vulnerabilities across maritime, rail, and overland corridors. The findings indicate that the core challenge facing global trade is not transport capacity, but rigidity in system design. By analyzing how different corridor types perform under geopolitical, climatic, and institutional stress, the paper establishes a conceptual basis for rethinking trade corridor design beyond single-route and asset-centered models.

title: Preference-Driven Contract Design: How Education Alters Risk, Patience, and Effort in Incentive Schemes

detail.title: Preference-Driven Contract Design: How Education Alters Risk, Patience, and Effort in Incentive Schemes
detail.abstract: Performance-contingent pay raises productivity, yet in the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) only about 16% of workers report receiving performance pay, with the incidence being roughly seven percentage points higher among university graduates than among non-graduates. This coexistence of low aggregate take-up and a strong skill gradient is puzzling. This paper accounts for these twin facts with a principal–agent model in which the entire preference vector—risk aversion, probability weighting, time discounting, and effort cost—varies systematically with schooling. Endogenizing preferences yields two predictions: (i) optimal incentive slopes and induced effort increase with education-linked preferences; (ii) the productivity threshold for accepting performance pay falls with schooling, while heterogeneity in tastes keeps worker participation incomplete. A light calibration guided by documented schooling gradients reproduces modest over all incidence alongside a pronounced skill gradient. The key novelty is to treat the preference vector as an endogenous state variable that enters both sides of the principal–agent problem, shaping the optimization problems of both the firm and the worker rather than being taken as a fixed primitive.

title: Commodity Price Volatility and Macroeconomic Transmission in Emerging Economies

detail.title: Commodity Price Volatility and Macroeconomic Transmission in Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: Commodity-exporting economies are highly exposed to external price fluctuations, yet empirical evidence on how commodity prices affect development outcomes remains mixed. This paper examines whether commodity price volatility operates primarily through macroeconomic transmission channels rather than direct growth effects in emerging economies. Using monthly data for a panel of commodity-exporting countries, the analysis applies unit-root tests, cointegration analysis, and Granger-causality tests to assess the relationships between commodity prices and key macroeconomic variables, including inflation, industrial production, and monetary aggregates. The results indicate limited and heterogeneous growth effects, but more consistent transmission through inflationary pressures and short-run macroeconomic instability, particularly in energy-exporting economies. These effects vary across countries, reflecting differences in macroeconomic structures and policy responses. The findings suggest that volatility management and macroeconomic coordination matter more than price levels for stabilising development outcomes. From a policy perspective, the results highlight the importance of volatility-aware fiscal and monetary frameworks in commodity-dependent economies, especially where exposure to external shocks remains high.

title:
Monetary Policy Under Uncertainty 
Why Expectation Management Is an Institutional, Not Mechanical, Problem

detail.title:
Monetary Policy Under Uncertainty 
Why Expectation Management Is an Institutional, Not Mechanical, Problem
detail.abstract: Expectations play a central role in modern economic theory and policy, yet they are almost universally treated as mechanical objects: probabilistic forecasts, equilibrium-consistent beliefs, or algorithmic updating processes. This paper argues that such treatments fundamentally mischaracterize the nature of expectations. Expectations are not mechanical responses to information; they are institutional commitments formed, stabilized, and revised within structured interpretive environments. The paper develops an institutional theory of expectation management, showing that economic coordination depends less on forecast accuracy than on the coherence, credibility, and legitimacy of the institutions that anchor collective belief. Mechanical models of expectationswhether rational, adaptive, or behavioral-fail to explain the stability of expectations in normal times and their abrupt collapse during crises because they abstract from the institutional scaffolding that makes shared expectations possible. Applying this framework to monetary policy, the paper demonstrates why forward guidance and policy communication frequently fail when institutional credibility is weak, and why expectation management cannot be engineered through signaling strategies alone. Extending the analysis to financial markets, asset pricing, liquidity dynamics, and systemic crises, the paper shows that market instability reflects expectation-regime breakdowns rather than forecast errors. Financial crises are interpreted as institutional transitions in which inherited interpretive frameworks lose authority, forcing agents to confront radical uncertainty without shared anchors. By reconceptualizing expectations as institutional phenomena rather than mechanical variables, the paper offers a unified explanation for the limits of policy communication, the dynamics of financial instability, and the persistent gap between formal economic models and observed market behavior. The analysis suggests that effective expectation management requires institutional coherence and narrative authority, not merely improved information or model sophistication.

title: PALESTAIN

detail.title: PALESTAIN
detail.abstract: This work critically examines the historical foundations of the Israeli state by interrogating dominant Zionist narratives through documented events, archival research, and testimonies from Israeli and non-Arab scholars. Beginning with the 1948 destruction of the Palestinian village of Tantura, the study highlights evidence of mass kills and forced displacement during the Nakba, drawing on Israeli academic research, forensic investigations, and survivor testimonies. It then deconstructs a series of core Zionist myths, including claims that Zionism represents Judaism, that Palestine was a “land without people,” that Britain opposed the Zionist project, and that Israel emerged as a weak state besieged by overwhelming Arab forces. By situating Zionism within broader European colonial and nationalist ideologies, the text argues that the establishment of Israel involved systematic ethnic cleansing, demographic engineering, and historical erasure rather than defensive self-determination. The analysis relies heavily on Israeli historians, official British documents, and international investigations to demonstrate how legal structures, military planning, and narrative control were employed to legitimize dispossession while silencing dissenting Jewish and Israeli voices.

title: Education in Yemen during the Armed Conflict: The Impact of Teachers' Salary Interruptions on the Quality of Education

detail.abstract: This research examines the impact of teacher salary cuts in Yemen during the armed conflict on the quality of the educational process, as one of the most important structural factors that contributed to the deterioration of the educational system during the years of conflict. Since 2015, the Yemeni education sector has faced overlapping challenges of infrastructure destruction, institutional breakdowns, mass displacement of teachers and students, as well as the near-complete or irregular payment of teachers' salaries. The research relies on a descriptive-analytical approach through a review of scientific literature, peer-reviewed studies, and reports Relevant international organizations. The results of the analysis show that the interruption of salaries directly contributed to the decline in the professional motivation of teachers, the decline in job stability, the high rates of absenteeism and dropout, in addition to the low levels of academic achievement of students. The research concludes that ensuring regular teachers' salaries is an essential input to improve the quality of education and rebuild human capital in Yemen.

title: Property Taxes and Rental Prices: Evidence from a Large-Scale Cadastral Reassessment *
affiliations: and Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile

detail.title: Property Taxes and Rental Prices: Evidence from a Large-Scale Cadastral Reassessment *
detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal effect of property tax increases on rental prices in Uruguay, exploiting a quasi-natural experiment from a large-scale cadastral reassessment in Canelones in 2011. Using a Synthetic Difference-inDifferences (SDID) estimator, we find the reassessment raised rental prices by 9.3% relative to a synthetic counterfactual, with effects becoming statistically significant three to four years post-implementation. The 21% average increase in taxable property values produced a pass-through rate of roughly 44%, consistent with incomplete adjustment in markets with inelastic housing supply. Leveraging housing demand elasticities from the existing empirical literature, our observed pass-through implies supply elasticities of 0.29-0.32, indicating relatively inelastic supply in Canelones' mixed urban-suburban-rural context. We also document a 12.4% rise in imputed rental values (valor locativo) for homeowners, reflecting broader market contagion. These findings highlight institutional constraints-particularly rental contract regulations that delay adjustment-influencing the timing and magnitude of tax pass-through, contributing to the literature on tax incidence in regulated housing markets and informing local fiscal policy design in federal systems.

title: Financial Risk Disclosure Return Premium: A Topic Modeling Approach

detail.title: Financial Risk Disclosure Return Premium: A Topic Modeling Approach
detail.abstract: We examine the risk factors disclosed in the 10-K financial statement section 1A across 9 years with over 500 hundred companies. We propose a financial disclosure risk factor to extend the Fama-French 3 factor model and Fama-MacBeth cross-section regression. Using the risk factors data from 2015 to 2023, we find the average risk-return premium across nine sectors is significant after controlling for other risk factors from the Fama-French 3-factor model. The premium is measured by monthly return series on risky-minus-less risky stocks or by the coefficient of stock risk factor estimated from cross-section Fama-MacBeth regressions. These text risk factors can potentially be used to construct portfolios that can generate significant returns across different sectors.

title: Systems Perspectives in Organization and Management Research: An Integrative Review and Roadmap for Meaningful use

detail.title: Systems Perspectives in Organization and Management Research: An Integrative Review and Roadmap for Meaningful use
detail.abstract: Systems perspectives offer a powerful alternative paradigm for understanding social phenomena as dynamic wholes characterized by emergent outcomes arising from interdependent interactions among diverse elements across multiple levels of analysis. Despite growing interest in systems thinking within organization and management (OM) research, much of its application remains ceremonial rather than meaningful, limiting the field's capacity to address complex, interconnected organizational challenges. This integrative review distinguishes three main types of systems perspectives-foundational, structural, and substantive-and examines how each can be leveraged to conceptualize phenomena, empirically investigate or simulate them, and develop theoretical explanations for their dynamics and outcomes. We trace the intellectual heritage of systems thinking and critically assess both its contributions and limitations, engaging substantively with critiques concerning cross-domain isomorphism, metaphorical overreach, ideological dimensions, and the obscuring of power relations. We identify conditions under which systems perspectives are most relevant, offer practical diagnostic frameworks and operational guidance for meaningful use across different epistemological traditions, and address the relationship between systems perspectives and adjacent theoretical traditions including institutional theory, organizational ecology, and practice theory. We acknowledge that systems research, like all research, serves particular interests and operates within specific epistemological commitments that shape what can be seen and said. By moving from ceremonial invocation to substantive engagement with systems perspectives, OM research can develop richer theoretical explanations and more effective practical interventions for the complex organizational phenomena that define our era.

title: Cryptocurrency Jump Contagion with Market Sentiment Events: A Study of High Frequency Cross Effect

detail.title: Cryptocurrency Jump Contagion with Market Sentiment Events: A Study of High Frequency Cross Effect
detail.abstract: This study aims to understand the contagion effect of the major equity market sentiment events, defined as jumps in the VIX index, on cryptocurrency price jumps and the corresponding feedback effect on investors' sentiment. Using recent high frequency intraday data with multivariate Hawkes processes, we find that several noteworthy contagion effects exist between Bitcoin and the market sentiment proxied by the VIX index. First of all, we find that positive market sentiment jumps tend to trigger a moderate level of cross-contagion on both positive and negative jumps in the Bitcoin market, whereas negative market sentiment jumps have no contagion effect on the Bitcoin prices. We also find that the Bitcoin market shows stronger positive self-contagion and cross-contagion effects than the equity market, in general. We also observe a lasting fear of missing out (FOMO) phenomenon in Bitcoin. It is supported by the evidence that the effect of positive jumps in the Bitcoin market lasts three times as long as that in both the equity market and the negative Bitcoin price jumps, and these positive jumps in Bitcoin may serve as a harbinger of equity market movement. These findings provide a better understanding of risk control and policy guidance for the cryptocurrency market.

detail.abstract: In complex social systems operating under sustained uncertainty, institutional stability depends not only on formal rule design but on the reliability with which institutions generate consistent, proportionate, and timely behavioral responses. This paper examines collective emotional regulation as a mechanism through which institutional reliability becomes observable in practice. Rather than treating emotional regulation as a diffuse systemic characteristic, the analysis conceptualizes reliability as an empirically traceable outcome manifested in enacted behavior, response timing, and proportionality under pressure. Drawing on developmental psychology, behavioral science, and institutional theory, the paper demonstrates how collective regulatory patterns are embedded in institutional action and how they differentiate formally similar systems in terms of functional performance. The study advances a conceptual framework for operationalizing institutional reliability as a behavioral parameter, enabling comparative analysis of governance capacity in complex environments.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a self-critical synthesis and comprehensive defense of the "Organizational Thermodynamics" and "Organizational Battery Theory" developed across five preceding works (the "Pentalogy"). While traditional econophysics has often been marginalized for its reliance on statistical analogies without microfoundations, the present framework redefines the economic system as a dissipative structure governed by thermodynamic necessity. By reinterpreting Walras' Law and integrating information theory, this paper addresses expected scholarly critiques regarding the internalization of the money market, the physical nature of financial capital, the limitations of the Modigliani-Miller theorem in frictional systems, and the empirical measurability of organizational entropy. We conclude that organizational survival is predicated on the Schrödinger Condition, establishing a physical "entropic boundary" that supersedes the "inflationary boundary" posited by Modern Monetary Theory (MMT).

title: Reachability and the Viability of Political-Economic Systems Under Stress: A Unified Law of Convergence and Divergence

detail.title: Reachability and the Viability of Political-Economic Systems Under Stress: A Unified Law of Convergence and Divergence
detail.abstract: Why do political–economic systems that appear strong, efficient, and unified often fail abruptly under stress, while others that appear fragmented or inefficient sometimes endure? Existing theories explain sources of stress or modes of failure but offer limited guidance on why responses to stress frequently accelerate collapse rather than prevent it. This article develops a structural invariant governing system survivability under stress, grounded in the concept of reachability. The argument holds that the long-run viability of any non-ergodic complex system exposed to propagating stress depends on preserving sufficient reachable states to reconfigure faster than stress propagates. From this invariant, the paper derives a unified structural result: excessive convergence (harmonization, centralization, standardization) and excessive divergence (fragmentation, loss of coordination) constitute symmetric failure modes that bound a narrow viability corridor. Systems exit this corridor either through correlated collapse or systemic paralysis. The framework reframes the debate between state capacity and sovereignty as a structural constraint rather than a normative trade-off and treats elite competition, ideological narrowing, and adversarial pressure as endogenous mechanisms of reachability loss. Historical stress tests and near-miss cases demonstrate consistent classification of collapse, paralysis, and survivability. The contribution is theoretical rather than predictive, specifying boundary conditions for governability over time.

detail.abstract: Motivated by recent studies that show that textual information contain economically meaningful information for asset prices, we examine the pricing of firms' forward-looking risk disclosures in the cross section of stock returns. We employ a generative AI model, an embedded topic model with FinBERT embeddings, to extract interpretable firm-level measures of narrative risk exposure from risk factor disclosures in 10-K filings of U.S public firms between 2010 and 2023. We construct textual risk factors from these disclosures and evaluate their pricing implications using portfolio sorts, Fama-French factor regressions, and Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional tests. We find that equity-focused financial condition risk earns a positive and economically meaningful premium of roughly 30-50 basis points per month, which remains significant after controlling for standard risk factors and multiple testing. In addition, covenant-focused financial condition risk, funding risk, and new product introduction risk exhibit statistically significant pricing effects in some specifications. Overall, our results indicate that the embedded topic model with FinBERT embeddings reveals more meaningful risks in narrative disclosures, and the firm-disclosed forward-looking risks are not fully priced by standard assetpricing models and that narrative financial-constraint measures earn incremental risk premia.

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with severe disruptions to healthcare delivery and a sharp deterioration in mental health, particularly among low-income populations. This study examines how the pandemic affected the utilization of prescription medications for anxiety and depression among Medicaid beneficiaries, a population especially vulnerable to both health and economic shocks. Using state-quarter Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data from 2014 to 2021, I estimate event study and difference-in-differences models to assess changes in mental health-related prescription use during the COVID-19 public health emergency. The results show that the pandemic was associated with a sustained increase in the share of all Medicaid prescriptions devoted to anxiety and depression, indicating heightened mental health burden among Medicaid enrollees. At the same time, prescriptions per enrollee for anxiety, depression, and all conditions declined, suggesting reduced utilization despite increased need. Differences across Medicaid expansion and non-expansion states highlight the role of insurance coverage in buffering access to care during systemic shocks. Relative to non-expansion states, Medicaid expansion states experienced higher prescription utilization and smaller declines in per-enrollee use during the pandemic. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of Medicaid expansion and program design in protecting access to mental health treatment during large-scale public health crises.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework conceptualizing wealth as a dynamic process driven by economic pressure disparities, drawing precise analogies from thermodynamics, electrostatics, and fluid dynamics. Wealth is redefined not as mere static accumulation but as value emerging from flows that bridge economic gaps, similar to lightning discharges or fluid movements across pressure gradients. Employing rigorous mathematical derivations, including stochastic differential equations and entropy maximization principles, we establish fundamental laws of financial dynamics, develop a multidimensional classification matrix for economic gaps, and critique illusions in static asset valuation. The model is substantiated by empirical evidence from econophysics, historical financial crises, and advanced agent-based simulations with complete Python implementations. Comprehensive sensitivity analyses, including global parameter variations, detailed Sobol indices with first-order, total-order, and interaction effects, and in-depth uncertainty quantification via Monte Carlo methods, demonstrate model robustness. This interdisciplinary synthesis provides deep insights into mechanisms of inequality, value creation, and economic stability, overturning conventional static paradigms and advocating policy measures for sustainable development. Innovative elements encompass financial entropy and potential functions, with applications to modern economies, thermodynamic integrations with climate economics, and extensions to Islamic economic principles for equitable growth. This enhanced version incorporates detailed computational tools and analyses to serve as a comprehensive resource for scientists and specialists in econophysics, thermodynamics, and economic modeling.

title: Scurramony: Deliberate Complexity as the Inverse of the Law of Parsimony

detail.title: Scurramony: Deliberate Complexity as the Inverse of the Law of Parsimony
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Scurramony (Jordan, 2026), a newly coined term describing the deliberate preference for unnecessarily complex solutions over simpler, functionally adequate alternatives. Scurramony is proposed explicitly as the inverse of the law of parsimony (Occam's Razor), which holds that, all else being equal, simpler explanations or solutions should be preferred. Unlike cognitive bias, which operates subconsciously, Scurramony concerns intentional action taken with awareness of inefficiency at the point of decision. While such choices are made deliberately, they may subsequently be transmitted and sustained through organisational culture, formal rules, or institutional inertia. The concept is defined, its scope delineated, and illustrated through examples drawn from film, labour relations, and public-sector decision-making.

detail.abstract: As part of the European Green Deal and the Fit for 55 package, the European Union has established a dual carbon market: ETS1, operating since 2005, and ETS2, which from 2027 will cover emissions from road transport, buildings, and small industries. This paper provides a forward-looking assessment of Italy’s emission trajectories under both systems and their alignment with the 2030 climate targets. A State–Space Model (SSM) is estimated for both ETS1 and ETS2 to capture the latent dynamics of emissions. Results show that ETS1 follows a structural declining trend, broadly consistent with the 62% reduction target, while ETS2 exhibits a persistent flat profile, reflecting the difficulty of decarbonizing the included sectors and falling short of the 42% reduction goal. To explore potential corrective pathways, a Monte Carlo simulation based on a differential equation is developed, integrating carbon price dynamics and technological uncertainty. Findings suggest that, without a robust and steadily increasing carbon price, ETS2 may reproduce the early inefficiencies observed in the history of ETS1. The proposed framework allows dynamic monitoring of emission trajectories and supports evidence-based policy adjustments, offering one of the first quantitative ex ante assessments of ETS2’s expected effectiveness.

title: Tracing the Funds: Designing a Three-Tiered Due Diligence Protocol to Mitigate Subcontractor Fraud in Federal Infrastructure Supply Chain

detail.title: Tracing the Funds: Designing a Three-Tiered Due Diligence Protocol to Mitigate Subcontractor Fraud in Federal Infrastructure Supply Chain
detail.abstract: The integrity of federal infrastructure supply chains is under persistent threat from sophisticated subcontractor fraud schemes, resulting in significant annual financial losses. Despite the critical nature of the public infrastructure, existing oversight mechanisms often rely on antiquated, "checkthe-box" due diligence that fails to penetrate the deep, fragmented layers of modern subcontracting. This study proposes a transformative Three-Tiered Due Diligence Protocol developed to move federal procurement from reactive "pay and chase" model to a proactive, data driven defense. Tier 1 establishes a digital parameter using Social Network Analysis (SNA) to identify "phoenixing" firms and beneficial ownership risks. Tier 2 implements a predictive filter, using the Altman Z-score to access financial distress and regression analysis to detect predatory patterns. Tier 3 provides a forensic shield through the integration of Internet of Things (loT) sensors and Benford's Law to verify that physical labor and materials align with digital invoices. Retrospective applications of this protocol to the I-35W Bridge collapse and the "Big Dig" project demonstrate that a stratified approach could have identified critical "red flags" prior to failure. By aligning these technical interventions with the legal rigors of the False Claims Act (FCA), this research provides a scalable framework for enhancing the resilience and transparency of infrastructure investments.

title: Why Policy Must Emerge From the Problem Space

detail.title: Why Policy Must Emerge From the Problem Space

declarations.funderStatement: No funding or institutional backing

detail.abstract: Modern governance systems are experiencing a widening failure of solution-generation. This failure is not primarily ideological, moral, or technological. It is structural. Decision-making authority has migrated outside the environments where consequences are lived, while incentives increasingly reward short-term optimisation over long-term coherence, reversibility, and baseline preservation. This paper proposes Open Source Governance as a structural response to this failure: a model where policy is developed, published, and iterated openly by those living inside the problem space, rather than being produced within captured institutional channels. It argues that a threshold has been crossed beyond which institutional solution-generation is no longer reliable, regardless of intent, competence, or political alignment. The paper draws together several previously published frameworks-including incentive cage analysis, baseline theory, reversibility constraints, algorithmic transparency, and sovereign economic design-into a unified governance model that prioritises coherence, human agency, and long-term system survivability.

title: Prospect Learning in Large Language Models: Quantifying Risk Preferences and Adaptation Dynamics

detail.title: Prospect Learning in Large Language Models: Quantifying Risk Preferences and Adaptation Dynamics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research uses only machine-generated data from large language models and does not involve human subjects. As such, an ethics review was not required according to standard guidelines.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research project.

detail.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cognitive proxies in behavioral and economic simulations, yet their underlying decision-making dynamics remain poorly understood. This paper introduces the Prospect Learning Framework (PLF)—a dynamic extension of Prospect Theory grounded in computational rationality—to assess whether LLMs express and adapt risk preferences over repeated choices. The PLF integrates classical loss aversion (λ) with three learning parameters—learning rate (α), behavioral drift (Δ), and outcome sensitivity (σ)—which together characterize belief updating, evolving risk posture, and responsiveness to recent outcomes.

Using twelve canonical Kahneman & Tversky (1979) lottery problems, we evaluate six persona-conditioned LLMs across four experimental settings (2,016 observations). Persona prompting produces large and systematic variation in risk preferences, with λ ranging from 1.0 to >6.0 (F = 181.17, p < 0.001). Learning rates vary sixty-fold (α ∈ [0.01, 1.36]), generating distinct adaptation profiles: herd-following personas exhibit Gambler’s-Fallacy-like behavior (σ = –5.9%), while loss-averse personas display Hot-Hand-style dynamics (σ = +7.3%). Replication across Llama 3, Gemma 3, Mistral, and Qwen 2.5 demonstrates architecture-invariant behavioral patterns.

Three findings emerge. First, LLMs do not naturally reproduce human Prospect Theory regularities, aligning with human choices only ≈50%. Second, persona conditioning provides a reliable and architecture-independent mechanism for steering risk preferences. Third, the estimated learning parameters reveal that LLMs adapt their behavior in systematic and predictable ways consistent with computational rationality—optimizing decisions within their representational limits.

The PLF offers a unified, reproducible framework for studying LLM risk behavior and establishes a foundation for constructing adaptive, heterogeneous agents in economic and social simulations. It reveals a structured behavioral landscape that mirrors core dynamics of complex adaptive systems, opening avenues for modeling emergent behavior, volatility, and feedback-driven adaptation in multi-agent LLM environments.
